Then $N_{n,k}\to\infty$, yet during every pause $Q_{n,k}/\sqrt{V N_{n,k}}=S_M/\sqrt{VM}>1$ is frozen above its typical value on a positive fraction of rounds, so no $\mathcal N(0,1)$ limit is possible. This is why the statement is formulated with the regularity $N_{n,k}/c_{k,n}\to1$, which is exactly what the Slutsky step consumes.
nodes.section: 7.3 Joint central limit theorem for the estimators
nodes.label: rem:componentwise_regularity

nodes.statement: Normalize arm $k$ by the \emph{deterministic} $\sqrt{c_{k,n}}$. By the Cramér--Wold device it suffices to treat a scalar projection $\sum_k w_k Q_{n,k}/\sqrt{c_{k,n}}$; since the arm indicators are disjoint, this is again a single martingale-difference array (row $n$ has increments $\sum_k (w_k/\sqrt{c_{k,n}})X_{i,k}(\xi_{i,k}-\theta_k)$), whose predictable variation is $\sum_k w_k^2 V_k N_{n,k}/c_{k,n}\to\sum_k w_k^2V_k$ by regularity, and which satisfies the conditional Lindeberg condition since $c_{k,n}\to\infty$. Theorem~\ref{thm:mart_clt} and Cramér--Wold give $(Q_{n,k}/\sqrt{c_{k,n}})_k\overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal N(0,\mathrm{diag}(V_k))$. The coordinatewise scaling $\sqrt{c_{k,n}/N_{n,k}}\to1$ in probability, so multivariate Slutsky transfers the limit to the self-normalized vector $(Q_{n,k}/\sqrt{N_{n,k}})_k$. Finally the Bahadur identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:estimator_bahadur}) and one more Slutsky step give the statement for $D_n(\hat{\Theta}_n-\Theta)$. \emph{Formalization.} \texttt{AlphaRAR.estimatorError\_joint\_tendsto\_multivariateGaussian}. The key device is that the weighted martingale array \texttt{AlphaRAR.wArray} carries \emph{row-dependent} weights $w^{(n)}_k = w_k/\sqrt{c_{k,n}}$, so one array covers both a common normalizer and per-arm ones; the Cramér--Wold projection is \texttt{AlphaRAR.wLinComb\_scaled\_tendsto\_gaussianReal}. Taking $c_{k,n}=n$ (with $N_{n,k}/n\to v_k>0$) recovers Corollary~\ref{cor:mart_clt_componentwise}; taking per-arm $c_{k,n}$ with limit $1$ gives the sparse form used in Chapter~\ref{chap:forced}. Note that a linear combination of \emph{random-time} sums is not itself a random-time sum, so the Anscombe route (Lemma~\ref{lem:anscombe_clt}) does not jointify; the martingale-array route above does, precisely because the arm indicators are disjoint.
nodes.section: 7.3 Joint central limit theorem for the estimators

nodes.name: CLT for the estimator
nodes.statement: Suppose $N_{n,k}/n\to v_k$ a.s.\ with $v_k>0$ for every arm $k$. Then, under Condition~\textbf{A}, $\sqrt n(\hat{\Theta}_n - \Theta)\overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal{N}(0,V)$ with $V=\mathrm{diag}(V_1/v_1,\dots,V_K/v_K)$.
nodes.label: lem:clt_theta

nodes.statement: Exactly as in Corollary~\ref{cor:mart_clt_componentwise}, but with the deterministic normalization $\sqrt n$ in place of $D_n=\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt{N_{n,k}})$. By the Bahadur identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:estimator_bahadur}), coordinate $k$ of $\sqrt n(\hat{\Theta}_n-\Theta)$ is $(Q_{n,k}/\sqrt{N_{n,k}})\cdot\sqrt{nN_{n,k}}/(N_{n,k}+1) + (\theta_{0,k}-\theta_k)\sqrt n/(N_{n,k}+1)$. The self-normalized martingale vector $(Q_{n,k}/\sqrt{N_{n,k}})_k$ converges to $\mathcal N(0,\mathrm{diag}(V_k))$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:mart_clt_joint_selfnorm}); the multiplicative factor tends to $1/\sqrt{v_k}$ and the additive one to $0$ in probability. Multivariate Slutsky then gives the diagonal rescaling $\mathrm{diag}(1/\sqrt{v_k})$ of the Gaussian, whose covariance is $\mathrm{diag}(V_k/v_k)=V$.

nodes.name: CLT for the plug-in target
nodes.statement: Under the standing hypotheses, $\sqrt n(\hat{\rho}_n - v)\overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal{N}(0,GVG^\top)$.
nodes.label: lem:clt_rho

nodes.statement: By the Taylor expansion (as in Lemma~\ref{lem:ell_rho_control}), $\sqrt n(\hat{\rho}_n-v)=G\sqrt n(\hat{\Theta}_n-\Theta)+O_p(1/\sqrt n)$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_theta} and Slutsky. \emph{Formalization.} The delta method is assembled in \texttt{AlphaRAR.clt\_rho}. First, Mathlib's product-space Slutsky lemma (\texttt{TendstoInDistribution.continuous\_comp\_prodMk\_of\_tendstoInMeasure\_const}) with $g(x,r)=Gx+r$ combines the estimator CLT (Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_theta}) with the fact that the first-order remainder $\sqrt n(\rho(\hat{\Theta}_n)-\rho(\Theta))-G\sqrt n(\hat{\Theta}_n-\Theta)=\sqrt n\,\varphi(\hat{\Theta}_n-\Theta)$ tends to $0$ in probability, and the limiting law is the linear pushforward of the estimator's Gaussian (\texttt{AlphaRAR.multivariateGaussian\_map\_matrix}, giving the covariance $GVG^\top$). The remainder-in-probability is discharged by \texttt{MeasureTheory.tendstoInMeasure\_smul\_littleO\_of\_tight} (an abstract $\varepsilon$--$\delta$ lemma: if $X_n=a_n\cdot S_n$ is tight, $S_n\to0$ in probability and $\varphi=o(\|\cdot\|)$ at the origin, then $a_n\cdot\varphi(S_n)\to0$ in probability), whose tightness input is supplied from the estimator CLT via \texttt{MeasureTheory.tight\_of\_tendsto\_probabilityMeasure} (portmanteau plus continuity from above of the limit Gaussian over $\{\|x\|\ge j\}\downarrow\emptyset$). The differentiability of $\rho$ at $\Theta$ (Jacobian $G$; Condition~\textbf{B}) and the a.s.\ consistency $\hat{\Theta}_n\to\Theta$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:LLN}) enter as the hypotheses \texttt{hTderiv} and \texttt{hcons}.

nodes.name: Asymptotic normality
nodes.statement: Under the generic conditions and Conditions~\textbf{A}--\textbf{B}, as $n\to\infty$: \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] for every $k$, $|N_{n,k}-n\hat{\rho}_{n,k}|=o_p(\sqrt n)$, $|N_{n,k}-n\hat{\rho}_{n,k}|=O(\sqrt{n\log\log n})$ a.s., and $N_{n,k}-nv_k=O(\sqrt{n\log\log n})$ a.s.; \item[(ii)] $\sqrt n(\hat{\Theta}_n-\Theta)\overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal{N}(0,V)$ and \[ \begin{pmatrix}\sqrt n(N_n/n - v)\\ \sqrt n(\hat{\rho}_n - v)\end{pmatrix} \overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow} \mathcal{N}(0,\Omega). \] \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: thm:normality

nodes.statement: Part (i) is Lemma~\ref{lem:prop_dev}. For (ii), the marginal CLT for $\hat{\Theta}_n$ is Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_theta}. By part (i), $\sqrt n(N_n/n-\hat{\rho}_n)=o_p(1)$, so $\sqrt n(N_n/n-v)$ and $\sqrt n(\hat{\rho}_n-v)$ have the same limit $\mathcal{N}(0,GVG^\top)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_rho}) and are asymptotically equal; the joint vector $(\sqrt n(N_n/n-v),\sqrt n(\hat{\rho}_n-v))$ therefore equals $(\sqrt n(\hat{\rho}_n-v),\sqrt n(\hat{\rho}_n-v))+o_p(1)$, which converges to $\mathcal{N}(0,\Omega)$ by Slutsky. \emph{Formalization.} Part (ii) is fully formalized for the $\alpha\text{RTS}$ design. The generic joint statement is \texttt{AlphaRAR.clt\_joint}: it takes the proportion-deviation fact $\sqrt n(N_n/n-\hat{\rho}_n)\to_p 0$ of part (i) as a hypothesis and assembles the joint CLT from \texttt{AlphaRAR.clt\_rho}. The joint vector is the image of $\sqrt n(\hat{\rho}_n-v)$ under the duplication map $x\mapsto(x,x)$ (the stacked matrix $[I;I]$) up to an $o_p(1)$ remainder, so the same product-space Slutsky lemma as in Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_rho} applies, and the limiting covariance $[I;I]\,GVG^\top\,[I;I]^\top$ is the block matrix $\Omega$ via the rectangular Gaussian pushforward \texttt{AlphaRAR.multivariateGaussian\_map\_matrix}. The self-contained $\alpha\text{RTS}$ instantiation is \texttt{AlphaRAR.aRTS\_clt\_joint}: from the same design bundle as \texttt{aRTS\_prop\_dev} plus the Condition-\textbf{B} differentiability of $\rho$ at $\Theta$ (Jacobian $G$, exactly the \texttt{clt\_rho} input), it \emph{discharges} the proportion-deviation hypothesis of \texttt{clt\_joint} from \texttt{AlphaRAR.aRTS\_prop\_dev} --- via the generic bridge \texttt{AlphaRAR.tendstoInMeasure\_toLp\_of\_forall\_isLittleOpOne} (coordinatewise $o_p(1)$ gives vector convergence in measure) and the $\sqrt n$-scaling identity $\sqrt n(N_{n,k}/n-v_k)-\sqrt n(\hat\rho_{n,k}-v_k)=(N_{n,k}-n\hat\rho_{n,k})/\sqrt n$ --- and derives the $\mathrm{thm{:}LLN}$ consistencies as in \texttt{aRTS\_prop\_dev}. Part (i) is fully formalized: the $o_p(\sqrt n)$ statement is \texttt{aRTS\_prop\_dev} and the two a.s.\ $O(\sqrt{n\log\log n})$ statements are \texttt{aRTS\_prop\_dev\_ae} and \texttt{aRTS\_count\_sub\_smul\_ae} (Lemma~\ref{lem:prop_dev}). Both parts of the theorem are therefore complete for the $\alpha\text{RTS}$ design.

nodes.name: Asymptotic efficiency
nodes.statement: When the arm responses belong to one-parameter exponential families with mean parameter, Proposition~\ref{prop:exp_fam} gives $V_k = I_k(\theta_k)^{-1}$, so the asymptotic variance $GVG^\top$ of $N_n/n$ equals the lower bound $G\,I(\Theta)^{-1}G^\top$ of \cite{hu2006asymptotically}, with $I(\Theta)=\mathrm{diag}(v_1 I_1(\theta_1),\dots,v_K I_K(\theta_K))$. Hence every $\alpha\text{RTS}$ design is asymptotically efficient.
nodes.label: rem:efficiency

nodes.name: Exploration schedule
nodes.statement: An \emph{exploration schedule} is a function $h : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] $\lim_{n\to\infty} h(n) = +\infty$; \item[(ii)] $h(n) = o(\sqrt n)$ as $n\to\infty$. \end{enumerate} (The Lean \texttt{AlphaRAR.IsExplorationSchedule} additionally records that $h$ is nondecreasing, a harmless convenience satisfied by the paper's examples that gives $h(\ell)\le h(n)$ for $\ell\le n$. It also \emph{weakens} (ii) to $h(n)=o(n)$: no result of the formalization uses $h(n)=o(\sqrt n)$ --- see Remark~\ref{rem:sparse_clt_fix} --- and the paper's condition survives only as the separate predicate \texttt{AlphaRAR.IsSqrtSmall}, which nothing assumes.)
nodes.label: def:exploration_schedule

nodes.statement: The D-Tracking choice $h(n) = (\sqrt n - K/2)^+$ of \cite{garivier2016optimal} violates condition (ii). The choice $h(n) = (n^{1/3} - K/2)^+$ satisfies both conditions and is used in the experiments.
nodes.label: ex:h_choice

nodes.name: Under-sampled and least-sampled sets
nodes.statement: For a schedule $h$ and $m\ge1$, \[ \mathbf{U}_m := \{ j\in[K] : N_{m,j} \le h(m)\}, \qquad \mathbf{S}_m := arg\,min_{j\in\mathbf{U}_m} N_{m,j}. \]
nodes.label: def:underexplored_sets

nodes.name: $\aRTSFE$ family
nodes.statement: Fix $\alpha\in[0,1)$ and a schedule $h$. A RAR procedure is in the $\alpha\text{RTS-FE}$ family if its allocation probabilities obey: \begin{align} \textbf{(Forced exploration)}\quad &\mathbf{U}_m\ne\emptyset \Rightarrow \forall a\in\mathbf{S}_m:\ p_{m+1,a}=\tfrac{1}{|\mathbf{S}_m|}; \\ \textbf{(Otherwise)}\quad &\mathbf{U}_m=\emptyset \Rightarrow p_{m+1}\ \text{satisfies the throttling condition \eqref{eq:throttle}.} \end{align} Like \texttt{AlphaRAR.IsARTS}, the Lean predicate \texttt{AlphaRAR.IsARTSFE} is stated on \emph{histories}, so it is a property of the algorithm alone; \texttt{throttle\_of\_isARTSFE} and \texttt{fe\_of\_isARTSFE} transport it to the process. It weakens \eqref{eq:fe_phase} to $a\notin\mathbf{S}_m\Rightarrow p_{m+1,a}=0$: uniformity on $\mathbf{S}_m$ is never used, only that no other arm can be drawn.
nodes.label: def:aRTSFE

nodes.statement: The full D-Tracking algorithm of \cite{garivier2016optimal} is the $\alpha\text{RTS-FE}$ member with $\alpha=0$ (up to the choice of $h$).
nodes.label: rem:d_tracking_fe

nodes.name: $\aRTSFE$ last hitting time
nodes.statement: For $k\in[K]$ and $n\ge1$, \[ \ell_{n,k}^{\mathrm{FE}} := \max\Big\{ m\le n : \tfrac{N_{m,k}}{m}\le\hat{\rho}_{m,k} \ \text{or}\ \big(\mathbf{U}_m\ne\emptyset\ \text{and}\ k\in arg\,min_{j\in\mathbf{U}_m}N_{m,j}\big)\Big\}. \] It is the last time before $n$ at which arm $k$ is under-sampled or is a least-sampled arm among the under-explored set.
nodes.label: def:hitting_fe

nodes.name: Sign after the $\aRTSFE$ hitting time
nodes.statement: For an $\alpha\text{RTS-FE}$ design and $m$ with $\ell_{n,k}^{\mathrm{FE}} < m \le n$, we have $\frac{N_{m,k}}{m} > \hat{\rho}_{m,k}$ and $\big(\mathbf{U}_m=\emptyset\ \text{or}\ k\notin arg\,min_{j\in\mathbf{U}_m}N_{m,j}\big)$; consequently $p_{m+1,k}\le\alpha\hat{\rho}_{m,k}$ (equal to $0$ during a forced exploration step in which $k$ is not least-sampled).
nodes.label: lem:hitting_fe_sign

nodes.statement: By maximality of $\ell_{n,k}^{\mathrm{FE}}$, neither disjunct in Definition~\ref{def:hitting_fe} holds at such $m$. If $\mathbf{U}_m\ne\emptyset$ then $k\notin arg\,min_{j\in\mathbf{U}_m}N_{m,j}$, so \eqref{eq:fe_phase} gives $p_{m+1,k}=0\le\alpha\hat{\rho}_{m,k}$. If $\mathbf{U}_m=\emptyset$ then \eqref{eq:fe_otherwise} and the over-sampling $N_{m,k}/m>\hat{\rho}_{m,k}$ give $p_{m+1,k}\le\alpha\hat{\rho}_{m,k}$.

nodes.name: $\aRTSFE$ satisfies the generic conditions
nodes.statement: For any $\alpha\text{RTS-FE}$ design, the generic conditions (Definition~\ref{def:generic_cond}) hold with $\ell_{n,k}^{\mathrm{FE}}$.
nodes.label: lem:preliminary_fe

nodes.statement: (i) Monotonicity and $\ell_{n,k}^{\mathrm{FE}}\le n$ are immediate. (ii) The telescoping identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:U_telescope}, whose proof only uses the increment of $U$) combined with Lemma~\ref{lem:hitting_fe_sign} — every intermediate $p_{m,k}-\alpha\hat{\rho}_{m-1,k}\le0$ — gives inequality \eqref{eq:generic_ineq}. (iii) At $m=\ell_{n,k}^{\mathrm{FE}}$, either $N_{m,k}/m\le\hat{\rho}_{m,k}$, giving $N_{m,k}-m\hat{\rho}_{m,k}\le0$, or $k$ is least-sampled in $\mathbf{U}_m$, giving $N_{\ell_{n,k}^{\mathrm{FE}},k}-\ell_{n,k}^{\mathrm{FE}}\hat{\rho}_{\ell_{n,k}^{\mathrm{FE}},k} \le N_{\ell_{n,k}^{\mathrm{FE}},k}\le h(\ell_{n,k}^{\mathrm{FE}})=o(n)$ by Definition~\ref{def:exploration_schedule}. (The paper bounds this by $o(\sqrt n)$ using condition (ii); $o(n)$ is all the consistency direction needs, and the $\sqrt n$-scaled direction gets a sharper bound from Remark~\ref{rem:sparse_clt_fix}.)

nodes.name: Validity under forced exploration
nodes.statement: Under Conditions~\textbf{A}--\textbf{B}, Theorem~\ref{thm:LLN} and Theorem~\ref{thm:normality} hold for every design in the $\alpha\text{RTS-FE}$ family.
nodes.label: thm:forced_valid

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:preliminary_fe} the $\alpha\text{RTS-FE}$ design satisfies the generic conditions with $\ell^{\mathrm{FE}}$; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:generic_main}. \emph{Formalization.} Both directions are \emph{direct reuses} of abstract-hitting-time theorems with the forced-exploration hitting predicate \texttt{AlphaRAR.aRTSFEUnder} (``under-sampled or under-explored''); the design enters as the history-level predicate \texttt{AlphaRAR.IsARTSFE} (Definition~\ref{def:aRTSFE}), whose throttle field is transported to the process by \texttt{AlphaRAR.throttle\_of\_isARTSFE}, and the only new ingredients are the forced-exploration smallness lemmas. So each of the five declarations mentions only the design, the environment and the schedule --- no process-level throttle hypothesis --- exactly as on the $\alpha\text{RTS}$ side. The consistency direction ($N_{n,k}/n\to v_k$, $\hat\rho_{n,k}\to v_k$) is \texttt{AlphaRAR.aRTSFE\_proportion\_tendsto} (reusing \texttt{AlphaRAR.consistency\_of\_hitting}), whose smallness is \texttt{AlphaRAR.aRTSFE\_smallness} ($N_\ell-\ell\hat\rho_\ell\le(h(\ell))^+=o(n)$). The asymptotic-normality direction (Theorem~\ref{thm:normality}) is: the $o_p(\sqrt n)$ deviation \texttt{AlphaRAR.aRTSFE\_prop\_dev} (reusing \texttt{AlphaRAR.prop\_dev\_of\_hitting}, smallness \texttt{aRTSFE\_smallness\_op}), the a.s.\ $O(\sqrt{n\log\log n})$ deviations \texttt{AlphaRAR.aRTSFE\_prop\_dev\_ae} and \texttt{AlphaRAR.aRTSFE\_count\_sub\_smul\_ae} (reusing \texttt{prop\_dev\_ae\_of\_hitting}/\texttt{count\_sub\_smul\_ae\_of\_hitting}, smallness \texttt{aRTSFE\_smallness\_upper}), and the joint CLT \texttt{AlphaRAR.aRTSFE\_clt\_joint} (reusing \texttt{AlphaRAR.clt\_joint\_of\_hitting}). Each abstract-hitting-time theorem is the generalisation of the corresponding \texttt{aRTS} theorem to an arbitrary measurable hitting predicate, with the throttle and smallness taken as hypotheses. Neither $\sqrt n$-scaled smallness lemma uses condition (ii): under Condition~\textbf{B} forced exploration eventually stops firing (\texttt{AlphaRAR.eventually\_sched\_lt\_pullCount}, the single-arm form of \texttt{AlphaRAR.underExplored\_eventually\_empty}), so past that time the hitting predicate can only fire through its under-sampling clause and the gap is bounded by a path constant (\texttt{AlphaRAR.aRTSFE\_gap\_le\_sum\_of\_not\_underExplored}) --- which is $o(\sqrt n)$ and $O(\sqrt{n\log\log n})$ for free. The Condition~\textbf{B} input is the consistency direction of this same theorem, so there is no circularity: it needs only $h(n)=o(n)$.

nodes.name: Forced exploration prevents starvation
nodes.statement: For any $\alpha\text{RTS-FE}$ design, $N_{n,k}\to\infty$ a.s.\ for every $k\in[K]$ (no assumption on the target).
nodes.label: lem:fe_no_starvation

nodes.statement: Suppose for contradiction that some arm $i$ stalls: $N_{n,i}=M$ for all $n\ge N$. Since $h(n)\to\infty$, enlarge $N$ so that $h(n)\ge M$ for $n\ge N$. Then for $n\ge N$, $N_{n,i}\le h(n)$ gives $i\in\mathbf{U}_n\ne\emptyset$, so the arm $I_{n+1}$ selected by forced exploration is a least-sampled arm of $\mathbf{U}_n$, whence $N_{n,I_{n+1}}\le N_{n,i}=M$ and $N_{n+1,I_{n+1}}\le M+1$. The potential $D(n):=\sum_j (M+1-N_{n,j})^+$ then satisfies $D(n+1)-D(n)=-1$ for all $n\ge N$, so $D$ becomes negative, contradicting $D\ge0$. Hence every arm is sampled infinitely often. \emph{Formalization.} \texttt{AlphaRAR.aRTSFE\_no\_starvation}, whose deterministic potential-function core is \texttt{AlphaRAR.no\_starvation\_pathwise}. It weakens ``$i$ stalls at $M$'' to ``$N_{n,i}<B$ for all $n$'' (arm $k$ monotone but bounded), and the action-level forced-exploration rule enters as the a.s.\ hypothesis \texttt{hfe} (when some arm is under-explored, $A_m$ is a least-sampled under-explored arm). The potential $D(n)=\sum_j(B+1-N_{n,j})$ is $\mathbb{N}$-valued (truncated subtraction is the positive part), so $D(n+1)+1=D(n)$ for $n\ge N_1$ forces $t\le D(N_1)$ for all $t$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Consistency and rate for sparse targets
nodes.statement: Under Condition~\textbf{A} only, any $\alpha\text{RTS-FE}$ design satisfies, for every $k$, \[ N_{n,k}\xrightarrow{a.s.}+\infty,\qquad \frac{N_{n,k}}{n}\xrightarrow{a.s.}v_k,\qquad \hat{\Theta}_n-\Theta = O\!\Big(\sqrt{\tfrac{\log\log N_{n,k}}{N_{n,k}}}\Big)\ \text{a.s.} \]
nodes.label: thm:sparse_rate

nodes.statement: The first statement is Lemma~\ref{lem:fe_no_starvation}. Given it, every arm's estimator converges: $\hat{\theta}_{n,k}\to\theta_k$ by the SLLN, so $\hat{\rho}_n\to v$ by continuity of $\rho$; the matching argument (as in Lemma~\ref{lem:match}, using Lemma~\ref{lem:convergence} and the generic inequality valid by Lemma~\ref{lem:preliminary_fe}) gives $N_{n,k}/n\to v_k$, allowing $v_k=0$. The rate is the LIL for the martingale $Q_{\cdot,k}$ scaled by its own sample size $N_{n,k}$, as in Lemma~\ref{lem:theta_LIL} but without dividing by $n$. \emph{Formalization.} \texttt{AlphaRAR.aRTSFE\_sparse\_rate}. All three statements flow from no-starvation (\texttt{aRTSFE\_no\_starvation}, $N_{n,k}\to\infty$): it makes every arm sampled infinitely often, so $\hat\theta\to\theta$ (\texttt{estimator\_ae\_tendsto\_of\_pullCount\_atTop}, \emph{no positivity}), whence $\hat\rho\to T(\theta)$, and the matching \texttt{consistency\_of\_hitting} (which never uses positivity, so allows $v_k=0$) gives $N_{n,k}/n\to T(\theta)_k$. The $N$-scaled rate is \texttt{AlphaRAR.abs\_estimator\_sub\_le\_rate\_loglog\_N}, which combines the exact Bahadur identity \texttt{estimator\_sub\_eq} with the subsampled loglog LIL \texttt{abs\_respMart\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_loglog} (this uses \emph{only} $N_{n,k}\to\infty$).

nodes.name: Componentwise CLT for sparse targets
nodes.statement: Under Condition~\textbf{A} only, any $\alpha\text{RTS-FE}$ design satisfies \[ D_n(\hat{\Theta}_n-\Theta)\overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal{N}\!\big(0,\mathrm{diag}(V_1,\dots,V_K)\big), \qquad D_n=\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt{N_{n,1}},\dots,\sqrt{N_{n,K}}). \]
nodes.label: cor:sparse_clt

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:fe_no_starvation}, $N_{n,k}\to\infty$ for all $k$. Given the regularity of the pull counts, Lemma~\ref{lem:componentwise} applies and gives the statement. \emph{Formalization.} \texttt{AlphaRAR.aRTSFE\_sparse\_clt}. Arms are split by a predicate $\mathrm{FEfed}$: \begin{itemize} \item if arm $k$ is eventually fed \emph{only} by forced exploration, then its count is regular against the \emph{deterministic} schedule, $N_{n,k}/h(n)\to1$ (\texttt{AlphaRAR.pullCount\_div\_sched\_tendsto\_one}); \item otherwise arm $k$ has a positive limiting proportion $v_k>0$ with $N_{n,k}/n\to v_k$, so it is regular against $v_kn$. \end{itemize} Both are then covered by the single per-arm normalizer $c_{k,n}=h(n)$ or $v_kn$, which is what \texttt{estimatorError\_joint\_tendsto\_multivariateGaussian} consumes (at $v\equiv1$). The split is unavoidable: not every arm can be forced-exploration-fed, since $\sum_kN_{n,k}=n$ while $K\,h(n)=o(n)$. The regularity for a forced-exploration-fed arm comes from a two-sided bound. \emph{Upper} (\texttt{pullCount\_le\_sched\_of\_fe\_only}): at a forced-exploration round the selected arm is itself under-explored, so one pull leaves it at $h(m)+1\le h(n)+1$. \emph{Lower} (\texttt{pullCount\_ge\_min\_sched\_of\_fe}): the selected arm is a \emph{least-sampled} under-explored arm, hence sits at the global minimum, so the potential $D(m)=\sum_j(L-N_{m,j})^+$ drops by exactly one per round while the minimum stays below $L$; since $D\le K L$ this can persist for at most $KL$ rounds, so within any longer window the minimum has reached $L$ or forced exploration stopped firing (which already means every count exceeds $h$). This is the same potential-function device as Lemma~\ref{lem:fe_no_starvation}. A mild regularity of $h$ itself is assumed (\texttt{hshift}: shifting the argument by the $O(h(n))$ catch-up window does not change $h$ to first order), satisfied by $h(n)=(n^{1/3}-K/2)^+$.

nodes.name: Scope of the sparse CLT
nodes.statement: The hypothesis that a sparse arm is eventually fed only by forced exploration is a genuine restriction, not an artifact. Since $T\ge0$ and $T(\Theta)_k=0$, the point $\Theta$ minimises $T_k$, so $\nabla T_k(\Theta)=0$ and $T(\hat{\Theta}_n)_k=O(\|\hat{\Theta}_n-\Theta\|^2)$. A design that \emph{chases} its target then allocates arm $k$ about $n\,T(\hat{\Theta}_n)_k\asymp n/N_{n,k}$ pulls, i.e.\ $N_{n,k}\asymp\sqrt n$ --- which dominates $h(n)=o(\sqrt n)$. For such designs (e.g.\ the distance-based example, where $\delta_{m,k}=(\hat\rho_{m,k}-N_{m,k}/m)^+>0$ keeps feeding arm $k$) forced exploration does \emph{not} set the scale, and whether $N_{n,k}/\sqrt n$ converges is a delicate question about the feedback between the estimator's own fluctuations and the sampling rate. By Remark~\ref{rem:componentwise_regularity} the conclusion cannot be obtained from $N_{n,k}\to\infty$ alone, so this case is genuinely open.
nodes.label: rem:sparse_clt_scope

nodes.name: Removing the forced-exploration-fed hypothesis
nodes.statement: The hypothesis discussed in Remark~\ref{rem:sparse_clt_scope} can be \emph{discharged} rather than assumed, at the price of reversing condition (ii) of Definition~\ref{def:exploration_schedule}. Replacing $h(n)=o(\sqrt n)$ by $\sqrt{n\log\log n}\ll h(n)=o(n)$ puts a sparse arm in the forced-exploration-dominated regime, where its count is regular against the deterministic schedule. Condition (ii) is in any case not needed elsewhere: under Condition~\textbf{B} forced exploration switches itself off (\texttt{AlphaRAR.underExplored\_eventually\_empty}), so $h(n)=o(n)$ suffices for the whole $\sqrt n$-theory --- and this is how Theorem~\ref{thm:forced_valid} is actually proved here, so no declaration of the formalization assumes $h(n)=o(\sqrt n)$. The reversed condition is satisfiable precisely where (ii) fails, e.g.\ $h(n)=n^{2/3}$ (\texttt{AlphaRAR.sched23\_satisfies\_schedule\_hypotheses}). \emph{Formalization.} \texttt{AlphaRAR.aRTSFE\_sparse\_clt\_of\_contDiffAt}: the conclusion of Corollary~\ref{cor:sparse_clt} with the forced-exploration-fed hypothesis replaced by the reversed schedule condition and $C^2$ smoothness of $T$ at $\Theta$. This is a deviation from the paper, not a formalization of it; the argument is written up in \texttt{maths/sparse-clt-fix.md}.
nodes.label: rem:sparse_clt_fix

nodes.statement: The normalization in Corollary~\ref{cor:sparse_clt} is componentwise (by $\sqrt{N_{n,k}}$) rather than by $\sqrt n$, which is what makes it meaningful when $v_k=0$. When $v\in(0,1)^K$ it recovers the classical result of \cite{hu2006asymptotically}.
nodes.label: rem:sparse_normalization

nodes.name: Pearson statistic
nodes.statement: Let $S_{n,k} := N_{n,k}\hat{\theta}_{n,k}$ and $\tilde{\theta}_n := \sum_{k=1}^K \frac{N_{n,k}}{n}\hat{\theta}_{n,k}$ be the pooled estimator. The \emph{Pearson chi-square statistic} is \[ \mathcal{X}_n := \sum_{k=1}^K \frac{(S_{n,k} - N_{n,k}\tilde{\theta}_n)^2} {N_{n,k}\tilde{\theta}_n(1-\tilde{\theta}_n)}. \]
nodes.label: def:pearson_stat

nodes.name: Quadratic-form rewriting
nodes.statement: With $Y_n := (\sqrt{N_{n,k}}(\hat{\theta}_{n,k}-\theta))_{k\in[K]}$ and $s_n := (\sqrt{\omega_{n,k}})_{k\in[K]}$ where $\omega_{n,k}:=N_{n,k}/n$, under $\mathcal{H}_0$ (common value $\theta$), \[ \mathcal{X}_n = \frac{1}{\tilde{\theta}_n(1-\tilde{\theta}_n)}\, Y_n^\top\,(I - s_n s_n^\top)\,Y_n. \]
nodes.label: lem:pearson_quadform

nodes.statement: Under $\mathcal{H}_0$, $\sqrt{N_{n,k}}(\tilde{\theta}_n-\theta) = \sqrt{\omega_{n,k}}\sum_j\sqrt{\omega_{n,j}}[Y_n]_j$, so $\sqrt{N_{n,k}}(\hat{\theta}_{n,k}-\tilde{\theta}_n) = [Y_n - s_n s_n^\top Y_n]_k$. Substituting $S_{n,k}-N_{n,k}\tilde{\theta}_n = N_{n,k}(\hat{\theta}_{n,k}-\tilde{\theta}_n)$ into Definition~\ref{def:pearson_stat} gives the quadratic form.

nodes.name: Idempotent projection
nodes.statement: For a unit vector $s\in\mathbb{R}^K$ (here $s=(\sqrt{v_1},\dots,\sqrt{v_K})$ with $\sum_k v_k=1$), the matrix $I - s s^\top$ is an orthogonal projection of rank $K-1$.
nodes.label: lem:projection

nodes.statement: $s^\top s = \sum_k v_k = 1$, so $(I-ss^\top)^2 = I - 2ss^\top + s(s^\top s)s^\top = I - ss^\top$, and it is symmetric; its trace $K-1$ equals its rank.

nodes.name: Asymptotic null distribution of the Pearson statistic
nodes.statement: Consider a RAR procedure with $N_{n,k}\to\infty$ a.s.\ for all $k$ (in particular any $\alpha\text{RTS}$ design under Condition~\textbf{B}, or any $\alpha\text{RTS-FE}$ design). Under $\mathcal{H}_0$, \[ \mathcal{X}_n \overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow} \chi^2_{K-1}. \]
nodes.label: lem:pearson

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:componentwise}, $\frac{1}{\sqrt{\theta(1-\theta)}}Y_n \overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal{N}(0,I_K)$ (Bernoulli variance $V_k=\theta(1-\theta)$ under $\mathcal{H}_0$). By Theorem~\ref{thm:LLN}, $\tilde{\theta}_n\to\theta$ and $s_n\to s=(\sqrt{v_1},\dots,\sqrt{v_K})$, so $I-s_ns_n^\top\to I-ss^\top$, an orthogonal projection of rank $K-1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:projection}. Slutsky's lemma and Lemma~\ref{lem:pearson_quadform} give $\mathcal{X}_n\overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow} Z^\top(I-ss^\top)Z$ with $Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_K)$, which is $\chi^2_{K-1}$.

Lemma~\ref{lem:pearson} shows that rejecting $\mathcal{H}_0$ when $\mathcal{X}_n$ exceeds the $0.95$-quantile of $\chi^2_{K-1}$ is asymptotically a level-$0.05$ test, valid for all $\alpha\text{RTS}$ designs (under Condition~\textbf{B}) and all $\alpha\text{RTS-FE}$ designs.
nodes.label: rem:test_level

nodes.name: Reduction to order one
nodes.statement: $X_n = o_p(a_n)$ if and only if $X_n/a_n = o_p(1)$, and $X_n = O_p(a_n)$ if and only if $X_n/a_n = O_p(1)$.
nodes.label: lem:op_factor

nodes.statement: Unfold Definition~\ref{def:op_Op}: both sides are the same statement about the sequence $|X_n|/a_n$.

nodes.name: Convergence in probability gives $o_p$
nodes.statement: If $X_n \to 0$ in probability (in particular, if $X_n \to 0$ a.s.), then $X_n = o_p(1)$. If $X_n \to c$ in distribution for some random variable, then $X_n = O_p(1)$.
nodes.label: lem:op_of_tendsto

nodes.statement: The first statement is the definition of convergence in probability. For the second, convergence in distribution implies tightness of the laws ($\{X_n\}$ is uniformly tight), which is exactly $O_p(1)$.

nodes.name: Arithmetic of stochastic orders
nodes.statement: For a fixed rate $a_n$: \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] $o_p(a_n) + o_p(a_n) = o_p(a_n)$ and $O_p(a_n) + O_p(a_n) = O_p(a_n)$; \item[(ii)] $o_p(a_n) + O_p(a_n) = O_p(a_n)$; \item[(iii)] if $X_n = O_p(1)$ and $Y_n = o_p(1)$ then $X_n Y_n = o_p(1)$; \item[(iv)] if $X_n = O_p(a_n)$ and $c_n \to c \in \mathbb{R}$ then $c_n X_n = O_p(a_n)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: lem:op_arith

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:op_factor} reduce to $a_n = 1$. Then (i)--(ii) are union bounds on the events $\{|X_n| > \varepsilon\}$, $\{|Y_n| > \varepsilon\}$; (iii) follows by conditioning on the tightness of $X_n$: for $\eta$ pick $M$ with $\sup_n \mathbb{P}(|X_n|>M)\le\eta$, then $\mathbb{P}(|X_nY_n|>\varepsilon)\le\eta +\mathbb{P}(|Y_n|>\varepsilon/M)$; (iv) is immediate from boundedness of $c_n$.

nodes.name: Slutsky bridge
nodes.statement: If $X_n \overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow} X$ (convergence in distribution) and $R_n = o_p(1)$, then $X_n + R_n \overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow} X$. More generally, if $(X_n) \overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow} X$ and $Y_n \to c$ in probability for a constant $c$, then $(X_n, Y_n) \overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow} (X, c)$.
nodes.label: lem:op_slutsky

nodes.statement: This is Slutsky's theorem, available in Mathlib as \texttt{TendstoInDistribution.prodMk\_of\_tendstoInMeasure\_const}, combined with the continuous mapping theorem \texttt{TendstoInDistribution.continuous\_comp} applied to addition.

nodes.name: Predictable quadratic variation
nodes.statement: Let $(M_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a square-integrable $(\mathcal{F}_n)$-martingale with $M_0 = 0$. Its \emph{predictable quadratic variation} is $\langle M\rangle := \mathrm{predictablePart}(M^2)$, the predictable part of the submartingale $M^2$ in the Doob decomposition. Equivalently, $\langle M\rangle_0 = 0$ and $\langle M\rangle_n = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}[(\Delta M_i)^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_{i-1}]$.
nodes.label: def:pred_qv

nodes.name: Increment of the quadratic variation
nodes.statement: For a square-integrable martingale $M$ with $M_0=0$, $\langle M\rangle_n - \langle M\rangle_{n-1} = \mathbb{E}[(\Delta M_n)^2\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]$, and $\langle M\rangle$ is nondecreasing and predictable.
nodes.label: lem:qv_incr

nodes.statement: The Doob decomposition of the submartingale $M^2$ has predictable part with increments $\mathbb{E}[M_n^2 - M_{n-1}^2\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}] = \mathbb{E}[(\Delta M_n)^2\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]$, using that $M$ is a martingale so the cross term $\mathbb{E}[2M_{n-1}\Delta M_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]=0$. Nonnegativity of the increments gives monotonicity.

nodes.name: Linear bound on $\langle M\rangle$ for bounded increments
nodes.statement: If $|\Delta M_i|\le c$ a.s., then $\langle M\rangle_n \le c^2 n$ a.s.
nodes.label: lem:qv_linear_bound

nodes.statement: Each increment satisfies $\langle M\rangle_{k+1}-\langle M\rangle_k = \mathbb{E}[(\Delta M_k)^2\mid\mathcal{F}_k] \le \mathbb{E}[c^2\mid\mathcal{F}_k] = c^2$; telescoping from $\langle M\rangle_0 = 0$ gives $\langle M\rangle_n \le c^2 n$.

nodes.name: $M^2 - \langle M\rangle$ is a martingale
nodes.statement: $M^2 - \langle M\rangle$ is an $(\mathcal{F}_n)$-martingale.
nodes.label: lem:qv_mart

nodes.statement: This is the martingale part in the Doob decomposition of $M^2$ (\texttt{martingale\_martingalePart}).

nodes.name: $\langle M\rangle$ is the unique compensator
nodes.statement: Call a process $A$ a \emph{compensator} of $M^2$ if $M^2 - A$ is an $(\mathcal{F}_n)$-martingale, $A$ is predictable, $A_0 = 0$, and each $A_n$ is integrable. Then $\langle M\rangle$ is a compensator of $M^2$, and any compensator $A$ of $M^2$ is indistinguishable from it: $\P[\forall n,\ A_n = \langle M\rangle_n] = 1$. So Definition~\ref{def:pred_qv}, which is a formula, defines the object the name describes, and does so up to the a.s.\ equality of paths that is the best any statement about conditional expectations can offer.
nodes.label: lem:qv_unique

nodes.statement: Existence is Lemma~\ref{lem:qv_mart} together with the predictability of the Doob predictable part (Lemma~\ref{lem:qv_incr}). For uniqueness, $M^2 = (M^2 - A) + A$ exhibits $M^2$ as a martingale plus a predictable process null at $0$, and the Doob decomposition is unique up to null sets (\texttt{predictablePart\_add\_ae\_eq}), so $A_n = \langle M\rangle_n$ a.s.\ for each fixed $n$; the index set is countable, so the countably many exceptional sets union to a null set.

nodes.name: Expected quadratic variation equals second moment
nodes.statement: For a square-integrable martingale $M$ with $M_0 = 0$ and every $n$, $\mathbb{E}[M_n^2] = \mathbb{E}[\langle M\rangle_n]$.
nodes.label: lem:qv_second_moment

nodes.statement: $M^2 - \langle M\rangle$ is a martingale (Lemma~\ref{lem:qv_mart}) starting at $M_0^2 - \langle M\rangle_0 = 0$, so its expectation is constant equal to $0$; that is $\mathbb{E}[M_n^2] - \mathbb{E}[\langle M\rangle_n] = 0$.

nodes.name: Martingale $L^2$ growth
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a square-integrable martingale with $M_0 = 0$. If every increment has second moment $\mathbb{E}[(\Delta M_{n+1})^2] \le \sigma^2$, then $\mathbb{E}[M_n^2] \le \sigma^2 n$.
nodes.label: lem:mart_sq_growth

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:qv_second_moment}, $\mathbb{E}[M_n^2] = \mathbb{E}[\langle M\rangle_n]$. Telescoping and Lemma~\ref{lem:qv_incr}, $\mathbb{E}[\langle M\rangle_n] = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\mathbb{E}[(\Delta M_{i+1})^2] \le n\sigma^2$.

nodes.name: Orthogonal martingales
nodes.statement: Let $M, N$ be square-integrable martingales such that $\mathbb{E}[\Delta M_i\, \Delta N_i \mid \mathcal{F}_{i-1}] = 0$ for all $i$ (e.g.\ if $\Delta M_i\, \Delta N_i = 0$ a.s.). Then $MN$ is a martingale, so the cross variation vanishes, and $\langle M + N\rangle = \langle M\rangle + \langle N\rangle$.
nodes.label: lem:qv_orthogonal

nodes.statement: $\mathbb{E}[\Delta(MN)_i\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}] = M_{i-1}\mathbb{E}[\Delta N_i\mid\cdot] + N_{i-1}\mathbb{E}[\Delta M_i\mid\cdot] + \mathbb{E}[\Delta M_i\Delta N_i\mid\cdot] = 0$, so $MN$ is a martingale (\texttt{martingale\_mul}). For additivity, expand $(M+N)^2 = M^2 + N^2 + 2MN$; the predictable part is linear and the predictable part of the martingale $MN$ vanishes, so $\langle M+N\rangle = \langle M\rangle + \langle N\rangle$.

nodes.name: First-order expansion with quadratic remainder
nodes.statement: Let $f : \mathbb{R}^K \to \mathbb{R}^d$ be $C^2$ on a convex open set $\mathcal{H}$, and suppose $\|\mathrm{D}^2 f(z)\| \le C$ for all $z$ in a convex neighborhood of $y \in \mathcal{H}$. Then for $x$ in that neighborhood, \[ \big\| f(x) - f(y) - \mathrm{D}f(y)(x - y) \big\| \le \tfrac{C}{2}\,\|x - y\|^2. \]
nodes.label: lem:taylor_first_order

nodes.statement: Apply the mean-value / Taylor formula to $t \mapsto f(y + t(x-y))$ on $[0,1]$: $f(x) - f(y) - \mathrm{D}f(y)(x-y) = \int_0^1 (1-t)\, \mathrm{D}^2 f(y + t(x-y))[x-y, x-y]\, dt$, and bound the integrand by $C\|x-y\|^2$. \emph{Formalization.} \texttt{AlphaRAR.norm\_sub\_fderiv\_le\_mul\_sq} states the equivalent bound $\|f(x)-f(y)-\mathrm{D}f(y)(x-y)\| \le K\|x-y\|^2$ under the (weaker, and here more convenient) hypothesis that the derivative is $K$-Lipschitz relative to $y$ on a convex set, $\|\mathrm{D}f(z)-\mathrm{D}f(y)\| \le K\|z-y\|$ --- which the second-derivative bound $\|\mathrm{D}^2 f\|\le C$ supplies with $K = C$ by the mean value inequality. The proof applies the mean value inequality \texttt{Convex.norm\_image\_sub\_le\_of\_norm\_hasFDerivWithin\_le'} on the segment $[y,x]$, where $\|\mathrm{D}f(z)-\mathrm{D}f(y)\|\le K\|z-y\|\le K\|x-y\|$ gives the constant.

nodes.name: Expansion of the target function
nodes.statement: Under Condition~\textbf{B}, there is a constant $C$ and a neighborhood of $\Theta$ on which $\big\|\rho(x) - \rho(\Theta) - G(x - \Theta)\big\| \le C\|x - \Theta\|^2$, where $G = \nabla\rho|_\Theta$. In particular, if $\hat X \to \Theta$ with $\hat X - \Theta = O_p(r_n)$, then $\rho(\hat X) - \rho(\Theta) = G(\hat X - \Theta) + O_p(r_n^2)$.
nodes.label: lem:taylor_rho

nodes.statement: Condition~\textbf{B} makes $\rho$ twice differentiable near $\Theta$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:taylor_first_order} applies with $y = \Theta$; the second statement follows from the order arithmetic of Lemma~\ref{lem:op_arith}.

nodes.name: Orthogonality of martingale increments
nodes.statement: Let $(M_n)$ be a square-integrable martingale. For $i \ne j$, $\mathbb{E}[\Delta M_i\, \Delta M_j] = 0$; consequently $\mathbb{E}[M_n^2] = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}[(\Delta M_i)^2]$ when $M_0 = 0$.
nodes.label: lem:slln_orthogonal

nodes.statement: For $i < j$, condition on $\mathcal{F}_{j-1}$: $\mathbb{E}[\Delta M_i \Delta M_j] = \mathbb{E}[\Delta M_i\, \mathbb{E}[\Delta M_j\mid\mathcal{F}_{j-1}]] = 0$. Expanding $M_n^2 = (\sum_i \Delta M_i)^2$ and using orthogonality kills the cross terms.

nodes.name: Weighted increment martingale is $L^2$-bounded
nodes.statement: Let $(M_n)$ be a square-integrable martingale with $M_0=0$ and $\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{\mathbb{E}[(\Delta M_k)^2]}{k^2} < \infty$. Then $S_n := \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{\Delta M_k}{k}$ is a square-integrable martingale with $\sup_n \mathbb{E}[S_n^2] = \sum_{k\ge1}\frac{\mathbb{E}[(\Delta M_k)^2]}{k^2} < \infty$.
nodes.label: lem:slln_weighted

nodes.statement: Each increment $\Delta S_k = \Delta M_k / k$ is $\mathcal{F}_k$-measurable with $\mathbb{E}[\Delta S_k\mid\mathcal{F}_{k-1}] = 0$, so $S_n$ is a martingale. By Lemma~\ref{lem:slln_orthogonal}, $\mathbb{E}[S_n^2] = \sum_{k\le n}\mathbb{E}[(\Delta M_k)^2]/k^2$, which is bounded by the convergent series.

nodes.name: $L^2$-bounded martingales converge a.s.
nodes.statement: A martingale $(S_n)$ with $\sup_n \|S_n\|_{L^2} < \infty$ converges a.s.\ to a finite limit.
nodes.label: lem:slln_l2_conv

nodes.statement: On a probability space $\|\cdot\|_{L^1}\le\|\cdot\|_{L^2}$ (\texttt{eLpNorm\_le\_eLpNorm\_of\_exponent\_le}), so the uniform $L^2$ bound gives a uniform $L^1$ bound, and $(S_n)$ is an $L^1$-bounded (sub)martingale. The $L^1$ martingale convergence theorem (Mathlib's \texttt{Submartingale.exists\_ae\_tendsto\_of\_bdd}) then gives a.s.\ convergence to a finite limit.

nodes.name: Kronecker's lemma, identity weights
nodes.statement: Let $(x_n)$ be reals such that the partial sums $\sum_{k<n} x_k$ converge (to some $s$). Then $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k<n} k\,x_k \to 0$.
nodes.label: lem:kronecker

nodes.statement: This is the special case $b_k = k$ of Kronecker's lemma, which is the only case used below (Theorem~\ref{thm:mart_slln}). Write $s_n = \sum_{k<n} x_k \to s$. Summation by parts (\texttt{Finset.sum\_range\_by\_parts}) gives $\sum_{k<n} k\,x_k = (n-1)s_n - \sum_{k<n} s_k$, so $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k<n} k\,x_k = \big(1-\tfrac1n\big)s_n - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k<n} s_k$. The first term tends to $s$ and the second is a Cesàro average of the convergent sequence $(s_n)$, hence also tends to $s$ (\texttt{Filter.Tendsto.cesaro}); the difference tends to $0$.

nodes.name: Kronecker's lemma, general weights
nodes.statement: Let $(b_n)$ be positive and nondecreasing with $b_n\to\infty$, and let $(y_n)$ be reals whose partial sums $\sum_{k<n} y_k$ converge (to some $s$). Then $\dfrac1{b_n}\sum_{k<n} b_{k+1}\,y_k \to 0$.
nodes.label: lem:kronecker_general

nodes.statement: Summation by parts: with $S_n=\sum_{k<n}y_k$, $\sum_{k<n} b_{k+1}y_k = b_n S_n - \sum_{k<n-1}(b_{k+2}-b_{k+1})S_{k+1}$. Dividing by $b_n$, the first term is $S_n\to s$; the second is a Toeplitz-weighted average of the convergent sequence $(S_{k+1})$ with nonnegative weights $(b_{k+2}-b_{k+1})/b_n$ summing to $(b_n-b_1)/b_n\to1$, each tending to $0$. Writing $S_{k+1}=s+\varepsilon_k$ with $\varepsilon_k\to0$ and splitting the sum at a threshold beyond which $|\varepsilon_k|<\delta$, the weighted average tends to $s$; the difference tends to $0$.

nodes.name: Bracket-weighted transform is $L^2$-bounded
nodes.statement: For a square-integrable martingale $(M_n)$ with $M_0=0$, the transform \[ T_n := \sum_{k<n} \frac{\Delta M_k}{1+\langle M\rangle_{k+1}} \] is a martingale (the weights $1/(1+\langle M\rangle_{k+1})$ are $\mathcal{F}_k$-measurable, as $\langle M\rangle$ is predictable), and it is $L^2$-bounded: $\mathbb{E}[T_n^2] = \sum_{k<n} \mathbb{E}\!\big[\tfrac{\Delta\langle M\rangle_k}{(1+\langle M\rangle_{k+1})^2}\big] \le \mathbb{E}\!\big[\tfrac1{1+\langle M\rangle_0}-\tfrac1{1+\langle M\rangle_n}\big] \le 1$, using $\mathbb{E}[(\Delta M_k)^2\mid\mathcal{F}_k]=\Delta\langle M\rangle_k$ and the telescoping bound $\tfrac{\Delta\langle M\rangle_k}{(1+\langle M\rangle_{k+1})^2}\le \tfrac1{1+\langle M\rangle_k}-\tfrac1{1+\langle M\rangle_{k+1}}$.
nodes.label: lem:slln_bracket_weighted

nodes.statement: The martingale property and Itô isometry give $\mathbb{E}[T_n^2]=\sum_{k<n}\mathbb{E}[(\Delta T_k)^2]=\sum_{k<n}\mathbb{E}[(\Delta M_k)^2/(1+\langle M\rangle_{k+1})^2]$; pull the $\mathcal{F}_k$-measurable weight out of the conditional expectation and use $\mathbb{E}[(\Delta M_k)^2\mid\mathcal{F}_k]=\Delta\langle M\rangle_k$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:qv_incr}). The telescoping bound holds because $(1+\langle M\rangle_k)(1+\langle M\rangle_{k+1})\le(1+\langle M\rangle_{k+1})^2$.

nodes.name: Bracket-normalized martingale SLLN
nodes.statement: Let $(M_n)$ be a square-integrable martingale with $M_0=0$. Then almost surely on $\{\langle M\rangle_n\to\infty\}$, $\dfrac{M_n}{\langle M\rangle_n}\to0$.
nodes.label: thm:mart_slln_bracket

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:slln_bracket_weighted} the transform $T_n$ is an $L^2$-bounded martingale, so $T_n\to T_\infty$ a.s.\ (Lemma~\ref{lem:slln_l2_conv}). Apply the general Kronecker lemma (Lemma~\ref{lem:kronecker_general}) pathwise with $b_k=1+\langle M\rangle_k$ (nondecreasing, and $\to\infty$ on the event) and $y_k=\Delta M_k/(1+\langle M\rangle_{k+1})=\Delta T_k$: $\frac1{b_n}\sum_{k<n} b_{k+1}\,y_k=\frac{M_n}{1+\langle M\rangle_n}\to0$, hence $M_n/\langle M\rangle_n\to0$.

nodes.name: Martingale SLLN
nodes.statement: Let $(M_n)$ be a square-integrable martingale with $M_0 = 0$ and $\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{\mathbb{E}[(\Delta M_k)^2]}{k^2} < \infty$. Then $\frac{M_n}{n}\to 0$ a.s.
nodes.label: thm:mart_slln

nodes.statement: By Lemmas~\ref{lem:slln_weighted} and \ref{lem:slln_l2_conv}, the series $S_n = \sum_{k\le n}\Delta M_k/k$ converges a.s. Apply Kronecker's lemma (Lemma~\ref{lem:kronecker}) pathwise with $b_k = k$ and $x_k = \Delta M_k/k$: $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k\le n} k\cdot\frac{\Delta M_k}{k} = \frac{M_n}{n}\to 0$ a.s.

nodes.name: Bounded increments
nodes.statement: If $(M_n)$ is a martingale with $M_0=0$ and uniformly bounded increments $|\Delta M_k| \le c$, then $\frac{M_n}{n}\to 0$ a.s.
nodes.label: cor:mart_slln_bounded

nodes.statement: $\mathbb{E}[(\Delta M_k)^2]\le c^2$, so $\sum_k \mathbb{E}[(\Delta M_k)^2]/k^2 \le c^2\sum_k k^{-2} < \infty$; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:mart_slln}.

nodes.name: Exponential supermartingale
nodes.statement: Let $(M_n)$ be a martingale with $M_0=0$ and increments bounded by $|\Delta M_i| \le c$. For $|\theta| \le 1/c$, the process \[ Z_n(\theta) := \exp\!\Big(\theta M_n - \theta^2 \langle M\rangle_n\Big) \] is a supermartingale, where $\langle M\rangle$ is the predictable quadratic variation (Definition~\ref{def:pred_qv}).
nodes.label: lem:lil_exp_supermart

nodes.statement: Using $e^x \le 1 + x + x^2$ for $|x| \le 1$ and $\mathbb{E}[\Delta M_i\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]=0$, \[ \mathbb{E}[e^{\theta\Delta M_i}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}] \le 1 + \theta^2\mathbb{E}[(\Delta M_i)^2\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}] \le \exp\!\big(\theta^2(\langle M\rangle_i - \langle M\rangle_{i-1})\big). \] Hence $\mathbb{E}[Z_i(\theta)\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}] \le Z_{i-1}(\theta)$.

nodes.name: Freedman-type inequality
nodes.statement: Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_exp_supermart}, for all $\lambda > 0$ and $v > 0$, \[ \mathbb{P}\!\Big(\exists n:\ M_n \ge \lambda \ \text{and}\ \langle M\rangle_n \le v\Big) \le \exp\!\Big(-\frac{\lambda^2}{2(v + c\lambda)}\Big). \] The formalized statement \texttt{AlphaRAR.measure\_exists\_ge\_le\_exp} is the pre-optimization, finite-horizon form: for each $n$ and each admissible $0<\theta\le 1/c$, $\mathbb{P}(\exists k\le n:\ M_k\ge\lambda,\ \langle M\rangle_k\le v)\le \exp(-\theta\lambda+\theta^2 v)$, obtained from Ville's maximal inequality (\texttt{AlphaRAR.smul\_measure\_sup\_le\_integral\_zero}) applied to the exponential supermartingale. Optimizing over $\theta$ and letting $n\to\infty$ recovers the displayed bound.
nodes.label: lem:lil_freedman

nodes.statement: Optional stopping applied to the supermartingale $Z_n(\theta)$ at the first time $M_n\ge\lambda$ with $\langle M\rangle_n\le v$ gives $\mathbb{P}(\cdots)\le \exp(-\theta\lambda + \theta^2 v)$; optimize over $0<\theta\le 1/c$. Equivalently, this is the Azuma--Hoeffding/Freedman bound that follows from the conditionally sub-Gaussian MGF machinery of \texttt{Probability/Moments/SubGaussian.lean}.

nodes.name: Optimized Freedman bound
nodes.statement: Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_freedman}, for $\lambda, v > 0$ with the admissibility condition $\lambda c \le 2v$ (so that the optimizer $\theta=\lambda/(2v)$ satisfies $\theta c\le 1$), \[ \mathbb{P}\!\Big(\exists n:\ M_n \ge \lambda \ \text{and}\ \langle M\rangle_n \le v\Big) \le \exp\!\Big(-\frac{\lambda^2}{4v}\Big). \] The variance proxy $2v$ (rather than the sharp $v$) comes from the one-step bound $e^x\le 1+x+x^2$, costing a factor $\sqrt2$ in the eventual constant.
nodes.label: cor:lil_freedman_opt

nodes.statement: Evaluate Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_freedman} at $\theta=\lambda/(2v)$, giving exponent $-\theta\lambda+\theta^2 v = -\lambda^2/(4v)$. The finite-horizon events increase to the event over all $n$, so their measures pass to the limit (\texttt{measure\_exists\_ge\_le\_exp\_all}).

nodes.name: Borel--Cantelli over blocks
nodes.statement: Fix threshold schedules $(v_k)_{k}$, $(\lambda_k)_k$ with $v_k,\lambda_k>0$ and $\lambda_k c\le 2v_k$, such that $\sum_k \exp(-\lambda_k^2/(4v_k))<\infty$. Then almost surely only finitely many blocks are ``bad'': for a.e.\ $\omega$, for all large $k$ and every $n$, $\langle M\rangle_n\le v_k \Rightarrow M_n < \lambda_k$.
nodes.label: lem:lil_bc

nodes.statement: By Corollary~\ref{cor:lil_freedman_opt}, $\mathbb{P}(s_k)\le\exp(-\lambda_k^2/(4v_k))$ where $s_k=\{\exists n:\ M_n\ge\lambda_k,\ \langle M\rangle_n\le v_k\}$. The right-hand sides are summable, so $\sum_k\mathbb{P}(s_k)<\infty$, and the first Borel--Cantelli lemma gives that a.e.\ $\omega$ lies in only finitely many $s_k$.

nodes.name: One-sided LIL, bounded increments
nodes.statement: Let $(M_n)$ be a martingale with $M_0=0$ and $|\Delta M_i|\le c$, and suppose $\langle M\rangle_n \to \infty$ a.s. Then \[ \limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{M_n}{\sqrt{2\langle M\rangle_n \log\log\langle M\rangle_n}} \le 1 \quad\text{a.s.}, \] and in particular $M_n = O\!\big(\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_n \log\log\langle M\rangle_n}\big)$ a.s.
nodes.label: thm:lil_bounded

nodes.statement: Fix $\eta>1$ and set $v_k = \eta^k$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_bc} with $\lambda_k=(1+\varepsilon)\sqrt{2v_k\log\log v_k}$: the tail bounds $\exp(-\lambda_k^2/(4v_k))$ are summable in $k$, so a.s.\ only finitely many blocks are bad. On the block $\{\langle M\rangle_n\in(v_{k-1},v_k]\}$ this yields $M_n < \lambda_k \le C\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_n\log\log\langle M\rangle_n}$; letting $\eta\downarrow1$ and $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ yields the $\limsup$ bound. \textbf{Formalization status.} The formalized statement \texttt{AlphaRAR.ae\_eventually\_forall\_lt\_dyadic} is the dyadic-block form: with the schedule $v_k=2^k$ and $\lambda_k = K\sqrt{v_k(k+1)}$ (where $0<K$ and $Kc\le2$, so admissibility $\lambda_k c\le 2v_k$ holds for \emph{every} $k$ via $k+1\le 2^k$, and the tail bounds $\exp(-\lambda_k^2/(4v_k))=\exp(-K^2(k+1)/4)$ form a geometric series), almost surely for all large $k$ and every $n$, $\langle M\rangle_n\le 2^k \Rightarrow M_n < K\sqrt{2^k(k+1)}$. This is the complete probabilistic content, built from Ville's inequality, the optimized Freedman bound (Corollary~\ref{cor:lil_freedman_opt}), and Borel--Cantelli (Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_bc}). Since on the block $\langle M\rangle_n\in(2^{k-1},2^k]$ one has $\sqrt{2^k(k+1)}\asymp \sqrt{\langle M\rangle_n\log\langle M\rangle_n}$, it gives the displayed $O(\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_n\log\langle M\rangle_n})$ upper bound, formalized in Corollary~\ref{cor:lil_upper} below. One deliberate deviation from the displayed statement remains unformalized: the $\log\log$ (rather than $\log$) rate with sharp constant $1$, which would require refining the one-step MGF bound $e^x\le1+x+x^2$ to variance proxy $1$ (valid only as the increment $\to0$). The $\log$ rate already gives $M_n=o(\langle M\rangle_n)$, which suffices for all downstream uses.

nodes.name: Normalized one-sided upper bound
nodes.statement: Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:lil_bounded} (in particular $\langle M\rangle_n\to\infty$ a.s.), there is a deterministic constant $C$ (depending only on $c$) such that almost surely \[ M_n \le C\,\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_n\,\log\langle M\rangle_n}\qquad\text{for all large }n. \] This is the consumable $O(\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_n\log\langle M\rangle_n})$ a.s.\ upper bound used downstream (Lemma~\ref{lem:U_increment_bound}, via the bounded assignment martingale).
nodes.label: cor:lil_upper

nodes.statement: Repackage Theorem~\ref{thm:lil_bounded}: for large $n$ let $k$ be the least index with $\langle M\rangle_n\le 2^k$. Minimality gives $2^k\le 2\langle M\rangle_n$ and $k\le\log_2\langle M\rangle_n+1$, so $K\sqrt{2^k(k+1)}\le C\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_n\log\langle M\rangle_n}$ with $C=K\sqrt{2(1/\log 2+2)}$, using $\log\langle M\rangle_n\ge1$ eventually.

nodes.name: Upper bound at scale $\sqrt{n\log n}$
nodes.statement: Under the hypotheses of Corollary~\ref{cor:lil_upper}, almost surely $M_n \le C\sqrt{n\log n}$ for all large $n$, for a deterministic constant $C$. This is the form $M_n = O(\sqrt{n\log n})$ a.s.\ used for the bounded assignment martingale $M_{\cdot,k}$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:U_increment_bound}.
nodes.label: cor:lil_upper_nat

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:qv_linear_bound}, $\langle M\rangle_n\le c^2 n$, hence $\log\langle M\rangle_n\le\log(c^2 n)\le 2\log n$ once $n\ge c^2$. Substituting into Corollary~\ref{cor:lil_upper} bounds $\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_n\log\langle M\rangle_n} \le\sqrt{2c^2}\,\sqrt{n\log n}$.

nodes.name: Truncated decomposition
nodes.statement: With $b_i:=\sqrt i$, set $\xi_i^{\mathrm t}:=\xi_i\mathbf{1}_{\{|\xi_i|\le b_i\}}$, $\xi_i^{\mathrm r}:=\xi_i\mathbf{1}_{\{|\xi_i|> b_i\}}$, $m_i:=\mathbb{E}[\xi_i^{\mathrm t}]$, $\tilde\xi_i:=\xi_i^{\mathrm t}-m_i$, and \[ \tilde M_n:=\sum_{i<n}\tilde\xi_i D_i,\quad R_n:=\sum_{i<n}\xi_i^{\mathrm r} D_i,\quad \mathrm{Dr}_n:=\sum_{i<n} m_i D_i,\quad N_n:=\sum_{i<n} D_i, \] so that $M_n=\tilde M_n+R_n+\mathrm{Dr}_n$.
nodes.label: def:lil_trunc

nodes.name: Summable tail probabilities
nodes.statement: $\sum_{i}\mathbb{P}(|\xi_i|>\sqrt i)<\infty$. (The formalized statement \texttt{tsum\_measure\_abs\_sub\_gt\_sqrt\_ne\_top} is the law-level version: for any finite measure $\rho$ on $\mathbb{R}$ with $\int(x-\theta)^2\,d\rho<\infty$, $\sum_i\rho(|x-\theta|>\sqrt i)<\infty$; apply it to the reward law $\rho=\nu_k$, $\theta=\theta_k$. This rests on a general-measure layer-cake bound \texttt{tsum\_measure\_Ioi\_ne\_top}, the $\mu$-general form of Mathlib's \texttt{tsum\_prob\_mem\_Ioi\_lt\_top}.)
nodes.label: lem:trunc_tail_summable

nodes.statement: Since $|\xi_i|>\sqrt i \iff (x-\theta_k)^2>i$, the sum equals $\sum_i\nu_k((\cdot-\theta_k)^2>i)$, which is finite by the layer-cake bound $\sum_i\mu\{X>i\}\le\int X\,d\mu+\mu(\text{univ})$ applied to $X=(\cdot-\theta_k)^2$ (integrable, being the arm-$k$ second central moment $\sigma^2$).

nodes.name: Tail is eventually zero
nodes.statement: Almost surely $|\xi_i|\le b_i$ for all large $i$; consequently $\xi_i^{\mathrm r}=0$ eventually and $R_n$ is a.s.\ eventually constant, so $R_n=O(1)$ a.s. The formalization has two layers. The abstract eventually-bounded clause \texttt{ae\_eventually\_abs\_le\_of\_tsum\_ne\_top} is stated for a general level sequence $b$ and takes $\sum_i\mathbb{P}(|\xi_i|>b_i)<\infty$ as hypothesis. The sampled version \texttt{ae\_eventually\_tailRespPart\_const} concludes that the tail remainder $R_n=Q_n-\tilde M_n-\mathrm{Dr}_n$ (\texttt{tailRespPart}) is a.s.\ eventually constant, via a \emph{conditional bookkeeping} step: the sampled tail event has $\mathbb{P}(A_i=k,\ \sqrt i\le|Y_i-\theta_k|)\le\nu_k(\sqrt i\le|\cdot-\theta_k|)$ (\texttt{measure\_action\_and\_tail\_le}, by conditioning on $\mathcal{G}_i$ and \texttt{condExp\_feedback\_comp}), so these probabilities are summable (\texttt{tsum\_measure\_action\_and\_tail\_ne\_top}, using the closed-window law-level bound \texttt{tsum\_measure\_abs\_sub\_ge\_sqrt\_ne\_top}).
nodes.label: lem:trunc_tail_const

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc_tail_summable} (in the sampled form above) the summability hypothesis holds, and the first Borel--Cantelli lemma (\texttt{ae\_eventually\_notMem}) gives a.s.\ that for all large $i$ arm $k$ is not sampled with an off-window response, whence $\xi_i^{\mathrm r}=0$ and the increments of $R_n$ (\texttt{tailRespPart\_succ\_sub}, where the truncated mean cancels) vanish for large $i$; a sequence with eventually-vanishing increments is eventually constant.

nodes.name: Truncated-mean bound
nodes.statement: $|m_i|\le \sigma^2/\sqrt i$ for $i\ge1$. (The formalized statement \texttt{abs\_integral\_truncation\_le} is the abstract single-variable bound: for a centred $X$ with $X^2$ integrable, $|\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{trunc}(X,A)]|\le \mathbb{E}[X^2]/A$; apply it to $X=\xi_0$ and $A=\sqrt i$.)
nodes.label: lem:trunc_mean_bound

nodes.statement: Since $\mathbb{E}[\xi_0]=0$, $m_i=\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{trunc}(\xi_0,\sqrt i)] =\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{trunc}(\xi_0,\sqrt i)-\xi_0]$, so by the pointwise bound $|\operatorname{trunc}(\xi_0,A)-\xi_0|\le\xi_0^2/A$ (the truncation is either $\xi_0$ or, off the window where $|\xi_0|\ge A$, is $0$ with $|\xi_0|\le\xi_0^2/A$), $|m_i|\le\mathbb{E}[\xi_0^2]/\sqrt i=\sigma^2/\sqrt i$.

nodes.name: Drift is $O(\sqrt{n})$
nodes.statement: $|\mathrm{Dr}_n|\le 2\sigma^2\sqrt{n}$ (everywhere, with $\sigma^2=V_k$). In particular $\mathrm{Dr}_n=O(\sqrt n)=o(\sqrt{N_n\log N_n})$ a.s.\ whenever $N_n$ grows linearly (the case of interest). The sharper bound $|\mathrm{Dr}_n|\le 2\sigma^2\sqrt{N_n}$ holds by reindexing to the sampled subsequence $i_j\ge j$, but is not needed and not formalized.
nodes.label: lem:trunc_drift

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc_mean_bound}, $|m_i|\le\sigma^2/\sqrt i$ (and $m_0=0$), so $|\mathrm{Dr}_n|\le\sum_{i<n}|m_i|D_i\le\sum_{i<n}|m_i|\le\sigma^2\sum_{i<n}\tfrac1{\sqrt i} \le 2\sigma^2\sqrt n$, using $\sum_{i<n}1/\sqrt i\le 2\sqrt n$ (\texttt{sum\_one\_div\_sqrt\_le}).

nodes.name: $\tilde M$ is a martingale
nodes.statement: $\tilde M$ is a martingale with $\tilde M_0=0$: $\mathbb{E}[\tilde\xi_i D_i\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}] =D_i\,\mathbb{E}[\tilde\xi_i\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]=D_i(\mathbb{E}[\xi_i^{\mathrm t}]-m_i)=0$, using that $\xi_i$ is independent of $\mathcal{F}_{i-1}$ and $D_i$ is $\mathcal{F}_{i-1}$-measurable. (Formalized in the \texttt{IsAlgEnvSeq}/\texttt{stationaryEnv} framework: $\tilde M$ is the \emph{truncated response martingale} $\tilde Q_{n,k}=\sum_{i<n}\mathbf{1}_{\{A_i=k\}} (\operatorname{trunc}(Y_i-\theta_k,\sqrt i)-m_i)$, a martingale for the action-augmented filtration $\mathcal{G}$. It is an instance of a general functional response martingale \texttt{genRespMart} --- of which the response martingale $Q$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:Q_martingale}) is the $g=\mathrm{id}$ case --- whose martingale property follows from \texttt{condExp\_feedback\_comp}.)
nodes.label: lem:trunc_mart

nodes.statement: Pull out the $\mathcal{G}_i$-measurable indicator $\mathbf{1}_{\{A_i=k\}}$; the conditional expectation of $g(Y_i)$ (with $g=\operatorname{trunc}(\cdot-\theta_k,\sqrt i)$) given $\mathcal{G}_i$ is $(\nu(A_i))[g]=m_i$ on $\{A_i=k\}$ (\texttt{condExp\_feedback\_comp}), so the centred increment has conditional mean $m_i-m_i=0$.

nodes.name: Quadratic variation of $\tilde M$
nodes.statement: $\langle\tilde M\rangle_n=\sum_{i<n}v_i D_i$, where $D_i=\mathbf{1}_{\{A_i=k\}}$ and $v_i:=\int(\operatorname{trunc}(x-\theta_k,\sqrt i)-m_i)^2\,d\nu_k$ is the truncated-response variance of arm $k$.
nodes.label: lem:trunc_qv

nodes.statement: Instance of the general functional quadratic variation \texttt{predQuadVar\_genRespMart\_eq}: the compensator increment is the $\mathcal{G}_i$-conditional second moment $\mathbb{E}[(\tilde\xi_i D_i)^2\mid\mathcal{G}_i]=v_i D_i$ (\texttt{condExp\_genRespMart\_increment\_sq}), and these sum to $\sum_{i<n}v_i D_i$. (Unlike the response martingale $Q$, whose constant variance gives $V_k N$, the truncated variances $v_i$ vary with $i$, so the weighted sum is retained.)

nodes.name: Quadratic variation upper bound
nodes.statement: $\langle\tilde M\rangle_n\le V_k N_{n,k}$ a.s., since each $v_i\le V_k$ (truncation reduces the absolute value, and variance is at most the second moment). This is the only bound on $\langle\tilde M\rangle$ used by the block LIL argument (the matching lower bound and the convergence $v_i\to\sigma^2$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc_var_conv} are not needed for the $O$-rate).
nodes.label: lem:trunc_qv_le

nodes.name: Truncated variances converge
nodes.statement: (Not needed for the $O$-rate.) $v_i\to\sigma^2$; in particular $\tfrac12\sigma^2\le v_i\le\sigma^2$ for all large $i$, so $\tfrac12\sigma^2 N_n\le\langle\tilde M\rangle_n\le\sigma^2 N_n$ eventually and $\langle\tilde M\rangle_n\asymp\sigma^2 N_n$.
nodes.label: lem:trunc_var_conv

nodes.statement: $v_i=\mathbb{E}[(\xi_i^{\mathrm t})^2]-m_i^2$. As $\sqrt i\to\infty$, $\mathbb{E}[(\xi_i^{\mathrm t})^2] =\int\operatorname{trunc}(x-\theta_k,\sqrt i)^2\,d\nu_k\to\int(x-\theta_k)^2\,d\nu_k=\sigma^2$ by monotone/dominated convergence, and $m_i\to0$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc_mean_bound}), so $v_i\to\sigma^2$. The upper bound $v_i\le\sigma^2$ is immediate from $|\operatorname{trunc}(\xi_i,\sqrt i)|\le|\xi_i|$.

nodes.name: Per-block Freedman with constrained $\theta$
nodes.statement: Fix $C>0$ and set $\lambda_k:=C\sqrt{2^k\,k}$. For each $k$, \[ \mathbb{P}\!\Big(\exists\,m\le 2^k:\ \tilde M_m\ge\lambda_k,\ \langle\tilde M\rangle_m\le\sigma^2 2^k\Big) \le \exp\!\big(-\tfrac{C}{2}\sqrt k+\tfrac{\sigma^2}{4}\big). \] Here $\sigma^2=V_k$ is the arm variance and $\langle\tilde M\rangle_m\le V_k 2^k$ uses only the upper bound Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc_qv_le}.
nodes.label: lem:trunc_block

nodes.statement: Apply the Freedman inequality (Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_freedman}) to the martingale stopped at time $2^k$ --- whose increments are bounded by $c_k=2\sqrt{2^k}$, so $\theta_k c_k=1$ is admissible --- with $\theta=\theta_k$, $\lambda=\lambda_k$, $v=\sigma^2 2^k$. The exponent is $-\theta_k\lambda_k+\theta_k^2\sigma^2 2^k=-\tfrac C2\sqrt k+\tfrac{\sigma^2}4$, since $\theta_k\lambda_k=\tfrac{C\sqrt{2^k k}}{2\sqrt{2^k}}=\tfrac C2\sqrt k$ and $\theta_k^2\sigma^2 2^k=\tfrac{\sigma^2 2^k}{4\cdot2^k}=\tfrac{\sigma^2}4$. Stopping at $2^k$ is needed so the increment bound holds up to the horizon; on the event only times $m\le 2^k$ occur, where the stopped process agrees with $\tilde M$. The formalization packages the stopping into a reusable device \texttt{AlphaRAR.measure\_exists\_ge\_le\_exp\_horizon}: a version of the pre-optimization Freedman bound (Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_freedman}) whose increment bound $|\Delta M_i|\le c$ is required only for $i<N$, and whose event is restricted to $m\le N$. It is proved by applying Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_freedman} to the deterministically stopped process $M^N_m:=M_{\min(m,N)}$ (Mathlib's \texttt{stoppedProcess} at the constant time $N$), which is a martingale (\texttt{martingale\_stoppedProcess\_const}), whose increments vanish past $N$ hence are globally bounded by $c$, and whose predictable quadratic variation agrees with $\langle M\rangle$ below the horizon (\texttt{predQuadVar\_stoppedProcess\_const\_of\_le}). Here it is used with $N=2^k$, $c=c_k=2\sqrt{2^k}$, the constrained $\theta_k=1/c_k$, and the increment bound $|\Delta\tilde M_i|\le2\sqrt i\le c_k$ for $i<2^k$ (\texttt{abs\_truncRespMart\_increment\_le}).

nodes.name: Block probabilities are summable
nodes.statement: For every $C>0$, $\sum_k \exp(-\tfrac C2\sqrt k+\tfrac{\sigma^2}4)<\infty$.
nodes.label: lem:trunc_block_summable

nodes.statement: $\exp(-\tfrac C2\sqrt k)$ is summable in $k$: since $\log=o(\sqrt\cdot)$, eventually $2\log k\le \tfrac C2\sqrt k$, so the terms are $\le k^{-2}$.

nodes.name: LIL for the truncated martingale
nodes.statement: $\tilde M_n=O(\sqrt{n\log n})$ a.s. \textbf{Reusable tool.} The block argument is formalized \emph{abstractly}, for any $L^2$-martingale $M$ with a square-root-growing increment bound $|\Delta M_i|\le a\sqrt i$ and a linear quadratic variation bound $\langle M\rangle_n\le v\,n$: the general lemmas \texttt{measure\_exists\_ge\_le\_exp\_block} (per-block Freedman), \texttt{ae\_eventually\_lt\_block\_of\_growing} (block Borel--Cantelli), \texttt{ae\_eventually\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_log\_of\_growing} (one-sided $O(\sqrt{n\log n})$) and \texttt{ae\_eventually\_abs\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_log\_of\_growing} (\emph{two-sided}, via $\pm M$ and $\langle -M\rangle=\langle M\rangle$) live in \texttt{LILTruncation.lean} and belong upstream. The truncated martingale $\tilde M$ is the instance $a=2$, $v=V_k$; in particular the two-sided form \texttt{ae\_eventually\_abs\_truncRespMart\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_log} ($|\tilde M_n|\le C\sqrt{n\log n}$) is free.
nodes.label: lem:trunc_mart_lil

nodes.statement: Borel--Cantelli over the blocks (Lemmas~\ref{lem:trunc_block}--\ref{lem:trunc_block_summable}) gives that a.s.\ for all large $k$ and every $m\le 2^k$, $\langle\tilde M\rangle_m\le\sigma^2 2^k \Rightarrow \tilde M_m<\lambda_k$ (formalized as \texttt{ae\_eventually\_truncRespMart\_lt\_block}, the summable first Borel--Cantelli step). To bound a fixed time $n$, take the \emph{least} $k$ with $n\le 2^k$; then $2^k\le 2n$ and $k\le\log_2 n+1$, and the quadratic-variation bound $\langle\tilde M\rangle_n\le V_k N_{n,k}\le V_k n\le V_k 2^k$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc_qv_le}) supplies the block hypothesis at $m=n\le 2^k$, giving $\tilde M_n<\lambda_k=C\sqrt{2^k k}\le C'\sqrt{n\log n}$. \textbf{Scale.} Because the increment bound $|\Delta\tilde M_i|\le2\sqrt i$ \emph{grows}, the block horizon $m\le 2^k$ forces the least admissible $k$ to satisfy $2^k\ge n$, so time-blocking delivers the \emph{time} scale $O(\sqrt{n\log n})$ rather than the variance scale $O(\sqrt{\langle\tilde M\rangle_n\log\langle\tilde M\rangle_n})=O(\sqrt{N_n\log N_n})$ of the displayed statement. The two coincide when arm $k$ is sampled a positive fraction of the time ($N_{n,k}\asymp n$, the regime of interest); the sharper variance-scale bound would require blocking by the quadratic variation rather than by the natural time, and is not formalized. The time-scale form is exactly parallel to the bounded-increment Corollary~\ref{cor:lil_upper_nat} (\texttt{ae\_eventually\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_log}).

nodes.name: Truncation to finite variance
nodes.statement: $M_n = O(\sqrt{n\log n})$ a.s. The formalized statement is \emph{two-sided}, \texttt{ae\_eventually\_abs\_respMart\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_log} ($|M_n|\le C\sqrt{n\log n}$ eventually, a.s.), with the one-sided form its immediate corollary. The two-sidedness comes for free from the reusable growing-increment LIL tool (see Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc_mart_lil}).
nodes.label: lem:lil_truncation

nodes.statement: By Definition~\ref{def:lil_trunc}, $M_n=\tilde M_n+R_n+\mathrm{Dr}_n$. The main term is $O(\sqrt{n\log n})$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc_mart_lil}); the tail is $O(1)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc_tail_const}); the drift is $O(\sqrt{n})$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc_drift}). Both remainders are $o(\sqrt{n\log n})$, so $M_n=O(\sqrt{n\log n})$. In the regime of interest $N_{n,k}\asymp n$, this is the $O(\sqrt{N_n\log N_n})=O(\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_n\log\langle M\rangle_n})$ rate (using $\langle M\rangle_n=\sigma^2 N_n$) required downstream.

nodes.name: $p$-series tail summability
nodes.statement: For every $\kappa>2$ and $\eta>1$, $\sum_{k}\exp\!\big(-\tfrac{\kappa^2}{4}\log\log\eta^k\big)<\infty$. (Formalized with base $\eta=2$ and the surrogate $\log(k+2)\asymp\log\log 2^k$: for $1<p$, $\sum_k\exp(-p\log(k+2))<\infty$.)
nodes.label: lem:llil_tail_summable

nodes.statement: For $k\ge1$, $\log\log\eta^k=\log(k\log\eta)$, so the $k$-th term equals $(k\log\eta)^{-\kappa^2/4}=(\log\eta)^{-\kappa^2/4}\,k^{-\kappa^2/4}$. Since $\kappa^2/4>1$ this is a convergent $p$-series (Mathlib \texttt{summable\_one\_div\_nat\_rpow}); dropping the finitely many indices with $\log\log\eta^k\le0$ does not affect summability.

nodes.name: Borel--Cantelli with eventual admissibility
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a square-integrable martingale with $M_0=0$ and $|\Delta M_i|\le c$ a.e. Let $(v_k),(\lambda_k)$ be positive schedules such that \begin{enumerate} \item $\lambda_k c\le 2v_k$ for all large $k$ \emph{(eventual admissibility)}, and \item $\sum_k\exp(-\lambda_k^2/(4v_k))<\infty$. \end{enumerate} Then almost surely, for all large $k$ and every $n$, $\langle M\rangle_n\le v_k\Rightarrow M_n<\lambda_k$.
nodes.label: lem:llil_evt_adm

nodes.statement: As in Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_bc}, for indices $k$ where admissibility holds the optimized Freedman bound (Corollary~\ref{cor:lil_freedman_opt}, infinite-horizon form \texttt{measure\_exists\_ge\_le\_exp\_all}) gives $\mathbb{P}(s_k)\le\exp(-\lambda_k^2/(4v_k))$, where $s_k=\{\exists n:\ M_n\ge\lambda_k,\ \langle M\rangle_n\le v_k\}$; for the finitely many remaining $k$ use the trivial bound $\mathbb{P}(s_k)\le1$. The total $\sum_k\mathbb{P}(s_k)$ is still finite, so the first Borel--Cantelli lemma (\texttt{ae\_eventually\_notMem}) places a.e.\ $\omega$ in only finitely many $s_k$; the complement is the claim. This is Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_bc} with its ``$\forall k$'' admissibility weakened to ``$\forall^\infty k$''.

nodes.name: Bounded-increment $\log\log$ exceedance
nodes.statement: Let $|\Delta M_i|\le c$ a.e.\ with $c>0$. Fix $\eta>1$ and $\kappa>2$, set $v_k=\eta^k$ and $\lambda_k=\kappa\sqrt{\eta^k\,\log\log\eta^k}$ (for $k$ large enough that $\log\log\eta^k>0$). Then almost surely, for all large $k$ and every $n$, $\langle M\rangle_n\le\eta^k\Rightarrow M_n<\kappa\sqrt{\eta^k\log\log\eta^k}$. (Formalized with $\eta=2$ and the surrogate $\lambda_k=\kappa\sqrt{2^k\log(k+2)}$.)
nodes.label: lem:llil_bounded_block

nodes.statement: Eventual admissibility: $\lambda_k c\le 2v_k$ reads $\kappa c\sqrt{\log\log\eta^k/\eta^k}\le2$, which holds for large $k$ because $\log\log\eta^k/\eta^k\to0$ (in the formalization, $\lambda_k c\le2\cdot2^k$ reduces to $(\kappa c)^2\log(k+2)\le4\cdot2^k$, eventual since $\log(k+2)=o(2^k)$). Summability: $\exp(-\lambda_k^2/(4v_k))=\exp(-\tfrac{\kappa^2}{4}\log\log\eta^k)$ is summable by Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_tail_summable}. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_evt_adm}.

nodes.name: General bounded-increment LIL, $O$-rate
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a square-integrable martingale with $M_0=0$, $|\Delta M_i|\le c$ a.e., and $\langle M\rangle_n\to\infty$ a.s. Then for every constant $C>2$, almost surely \[ M_n\le C\,\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_n\,\log\log\langle M\rangle_n}\qquad \text{for all large }n. \]
nodes.label: thm:llil_bounded

nodes.statement: Pick $\eta>1$ and $\kappa\in(2,C/\sqrt\eta)$ (possible once $\eta<(C/2)^2$), and use Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_bounded_block}. For large $n$ let $k$ be the least index with $\langle M\rangle_n\le\eta^k$; minimality gives $\eta^k\le\eta\langle M\rangle_n$, and $\langle M\rangle_n\to\infty$ makes $\log\log\eta^k\le\log\log(\eta\langle M\rangle_n) \le(1+o(1))\log\log\langle M\rangle_n$. Hence $M_n<\kappa\sqrt{\eta^k\log\log\eta^k}\le\kappa\sqrt\eta\,(1+o(1)) \sqrt{\langle M\rangle_n\log\log\langle M\rangle_n}\le C\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_n \log\log\langle M\rangle_n}$ for large $n$.

nodes.name: Condition \textbf{(H)}
nodes.statement: $M$ satisfies \textbf{(H)} with constant $A>0$ if there is an $\mathcal{F}$-predictable sequence $(c_i)$ with $|\Delta M_i|\le c_i$ a.e.\ and, for all large $i$, \[ c_i\ \le\ A\,\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_i\,/\,\log\log\langle M\rangle_i}\qquad\text{a.e.} \]
nodes.section: 13.2 The general hypothesis: small increments on the LIL scale
nodes.label: def:llil_H

nodes.name: Quadratic-variation stopping
nodes.statement: This is the standard device of the martingale LIL \cite{Stout1970,HallHeyde1980} (see also \cite{Freedman1975} for the underlying exponential inequality): the geometric \emph{block base} must act on the quadratic variation itself (via a random stopping time), \emph{not} on a deterministic time horizon. A deterministic-horizon blocking $2^j$ (as in the $O$-rate engine of Chapter~\ref{chap:pre_lil}) unavoidably loses a factor $\sqrt2$ in the constant when passing to the $\langle M\rangle_n$ scale, so it yields the $O$-rate but never the sharp constant~$1$; the sharp constant requires block base $\eta\downarrow1$ on $\langle M\rangle$, which is exactly this quadratic-variation stopping. For $v>0$ let $\tau_v:=\inf\{n:\ \langle M\rangle_{n+1}>v\}$. Because $\langle M\rangle$ is predictable ($\langle M\rangle_{n+1}$ is $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable), $\tau_v$ is a stopping time, and on $\{n\le\tau_v\}$ one has $\langle M\rangle_n\le v$. The stopped process $M^{\tau_v}_n:=M_{n\wedge\tau_v}$ is a martingale with $\langle M^{\tau_v}\rangle_n=\langle M\rangle_{n\wedge\tau_v}$, and under \textbf{(H)} with constant $A$ its increments obey $|\Delta M^{\tau_v}_i|\le C(v):=A\sqrt{v/\log\log v}$ a.e.\ for all $i$ (for $v$ large), since for $i<\tau_v$ we have $\langle M\rangle_i\le v$ and past $\tau_v$ the increments vanish. Moreover \[ \{\exists n:\ M_n\ge\lambda,\ \langle M\rangle_n\le v\}\ \subseteq\ \{\exists n:\ M^{\tau_v}_n\ge\lambda,\ \langle M^{\tau_v}\rangle_n\le v\}. \]
nodes.section: 13.2 The general hypothesis: small increments on the LIL scale
nodes.label: lem:llil_qv_stop

nodes.statement: Predictability of $\langle M\rangle$ gives $\{\tau_v\ge n+1\}=\{\langle M\rangle_{n+1} \le v\}\in\mathcal{F}_n$, so $\tau_v$ is a stopping time (constructible with Mathlib's \texttt{hittingBtwn}, the stopping-time API already used in the proof of Ville's inequality). That $M^{\tau_v}$ is a martingale is Mathlib's \texttt{Submartingale.stoppedProcess} applied to $\pm M$; the increment bound uses monotonicity of $\langle M\rangle$ and \textbf{(H)}. The only genuinely new ingredient is the quadratic-variation identity $\langle M^{\tau_v}\rangle=\langle M\rangle_{\cdot\wedge \tau_v}$, the stopping-time analogue of the \emph{formalized} deterministic-horizon \texttt{predQuadVar\_stoppedProcess\_const\_of\_le} of Chapter~\ref{chap:pre_lil}. For the inclusion: if $\langle M\rangle_n\le v$ then $n\le\tau_v$, so $M^{\tau_v}_n=M_n$ and $\langle M^{\tau_v}\rangle_n=\langle M\rangle_n$.
nodes.section: 13.2 The general hypothesis: small increments on the LIL scale

nodes.name: Per-block bound under \textbf{(H)}
nodes.statement: Suppose $M$ satisfies \textbf{(H)} with constant $A$. Fix $\kappa>0$ with $\kappa A\le2$, set $v_k=\eta^k$ ($\eta>1$) and $\lambda_k=\kappa\sqrt{v_k\log\log v_k}$. Then for all large $k$, \[ \mathbb{P}\big(\exists n:\ M_n\ge\lambda_k,\ \langle M\rangle_n\le v_k\big)\ \le\ \exp\!\big(-\tfrac{\kappa^2}{4}\log\log v_k\big). \]
nodes.section: 13.2 The general hypothesis: small increments on the LIL scale
nodes.label: lem:llil_H_measure

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_qv_stop} the event is contained in the corresponding event for the stopped martingale $M^{\tau_{v_k}}$, whose increments are globally bounded by $C(v_k)=A\sqrt{v_k/\log\log v_k}$. Apply the optimized infinite-horizon Freedman bound (Corollary~\ref{cor:lil_freedman_opt}) to $M^{\tau_{v_k}}$ with $c=C(v_k)$, $\lambda=\lambda_k$, $v=v_k$: admissibility $\lambda_k C(v_k)\le2v_k$ reads $\kappa\sqrt{v_k\log\log v_k}\cdot A\sqrt{v_k/\log\log v_k}=\kappa A\,v_k\le2v_k$, i.e.\ $\kappa A\le2$; and the exponent is $-\lambda_k^2/(4v_k)=-\tfrac{\kappa^2}{4}\log\log v_k$.
nodes.section: 13.2 The general hypothesis: small increments on the LIL scale

nodes.name: \textbf{(H)} exceedance
nodes.statement: Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_H_measure} with additionally $\kappa>2$ (so $A<1$ and $A\le2/\kappa$), almost surely for all large $k$ and every $n$, $\langle M\rangle_n\le\eta^k\Rightarrow M_n<\kappa\sqrt{\eta^k\log\log\eta^k}$.
nodes.section: 13.2 The general hypothesis: small increments on the LIL scale
nodes.label: lem:llil_H_block

nodes.statement: The per-block bounds of Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_H_measure} are summable by Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_tail_summable} ($\kappa>2$), so $\sum_k\mathbb{P}(s_k)<\infty$ with $s_k=\{\exists n:\ M_n\ge\lambda_k,\ \langle M\rangle_n\le v_k\}$; the first Borel--Cantelli lemma finishes as in Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_evt_adm}.
nodes.section: 13.2 The general hypothesis: small increments on the LIL scale

nodes.name: General martingale LIL under \textbf{(H)}, $O$-rate
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a square-integrable martingale with $M_0=0$ satisfying \textbf{(H)} with some constant $A<1$, and $\langle M\rangle_n\to\infty$ a.s. Then there is a constant $C$ (any $C>2$ suffices, once $A$ is small enough) such that almost surely \[ M_n\le C\,\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_n\,\log\log\langle M\rangle_n}\qquad \text{for all large }n. \] Bounded increments (Theorem~\ref{thm:llil_bounded}) are the case $A\to0$.
nodes.section: 13.2 The general hypothesis: small increments on the LIL scale
nodes.label: thm:llil_general

nodes.statement: Choose $\kappa>2$ with $\kappa A\le2$ and $\eta>1$, apply Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_H_block}, and repackage exactly as in Theorem~\ref{thm:llil_bounded} (least $k$ with $\langle M\rangle_n\le\eta^k$).
nodes.section: 13.2 The general hypothesis: small increments on the LIL scale

nodes.name: Refined elementary inequality
nodes.statement: For every $\delta>0$ there is $\eta_\delta>0$ such that $e^x\le1+x+\tfrac12(1+\delta)x^2$ for all $|x|\le\eta_\delta$.
nodes.label: lem:llil_refined_ineq

nodes.statement: Mathlib's \texttt{Real.exp\_bound} at $n=3$ gives, for $|x|\le1$, $\big|e^x-(1+x+\tfrac12 x^2)\big|\le|x|^3\cdot\tfrac{4}{3!\cdot3}=\tfrac29|x|^3$, hence $e^x\le1+x+\tfrac12 x^2+\tfrac29|x|^3\le1+x+\tfrac12\big(1+\tfrac49|x|\big)x^2$; take $\eta_\delta:=\min(1,\tfrac94\delta)$. (So this lemma is a Mathlib one-liner, not new work.)

nodes.name: Refined conditional MGF bound
nodes.statement: If $|\Delta M_i|\le c$ a.e.\ and $|\theta|c\le\eta_\delta$, then $\mathbb{E}[e^{\theta\Delta M_i}\mid\mathcal{F}_i]\le\exp\!\big(\tfrac12(1+\delta)\theta^2 (\langle M\rangle_{i+1}-\langle M\rangle_i)\big)$ a.e.
nodes.label: lem:llil_refined_mgf

nodes.statement: As in Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_exp_supermart}'s one-step bound, but with Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_refined_ineq} in place of $e^x\le1+x+x^2$: using $\mathbb{E}[\Delta M_i\mid\mathcal{F}_i]=0$ and $\mathbb{E}[(\Delta M_i)^2\mid\mathcal{F}_i]=\langle M\rangle_{i+1} -\langle M\rangle_i$, one gets $\mathbb{E}[e^{\theta\Delta M_i}\mid\mathcal{F}_i]\le1+\tfrac12(1+\delta)\theta^2 (\langle M\rangle_{i+1}-\langle M\rangle_i)\le\exp(\cdots)$.

nodes.name: Refined exponential supermartingale and Freedman bound
nodes.statement: Under $|\Delta M_i|\le c$ and $|\theta|c\le\eta_\delta$, the process $Z_n=\exp\!\big(\theta M_n-\tfrac12(1+\delta)\theta^2\langle M\rangle_n\big)$ is a supermartingale, and hence for $\lambda,v>0$, \[ \mathbb{P}\big(\exists n:\ M_n\ge\lambda,\ \langle M\rangle_n\le v\big)\ \le\ \exp\!\big(-\theta\lambda+\tfrac12(1+\delta)\theta^2 v\big). \] Optimizing at $\theta=\lambda/((1+\delta)v)$ (admissible when $\lambda c\le(1+\delta)v\,\eta_\delta$) gives the bound $\exp\!\big(-\lambda^2/(2(1+\delta)v)\big)$.
nodes.label: lem:llil_refined_freedman

nodes.statement: Verbatim the proofs of Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_exp_supermart} (supermartingale, via Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_refined_mgf}), Lemma~\ref{lem:lil_freedman} (Ville's inequality), and Corollary~\ref{cor:lil_freedman_opt} (optimization), with the proxy $2v$ replaced by $(1+\delta)v$.

nodes.name: Sharp exceedance
nodes.statement: Let $M$ satisfy \textbf{(H)} with constant $A$ (or have bounded increments), and $\langle M\rangle_n\to\infty$. Fix $\eta>1$ and $\varepsilon>\delta>0$, set $v_k=\eta^k$ and $\lambda_k=\sqrt{2(1+\varepsilon)\,v_k\log\log v_k}$. Then almost surely for all large $k$ and every $n$, $\langle M\rangle_n\le\eta^k\Rightarrow M_n<\sqrt{2(1+\varepsilon)\eta^k\log\log\eta^k}$. (Formalized for bounded increments, with the surrogate $\log(k+2)\asymp\log\log\eta^k$ in place of $\log\log\eta^k$, which is asymptotically equal and so preserves the sharp constant.)
nodes.label: lem:llil_sharp_block

nodes.statement: Stop at $\tau_{v_k}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_qv_stop}); the stopped increments are bounded by $C(v_k)=A\sqrt{v_k/\log\log v_k}$ (or by the fixed $c$). The optimizer $\theta_k=\lambda_k/((1+\delta)v_k)=\sqrt{2(1+\varepsilon)\log\log v_k/v_k}/(1+\delta)$ satisfies $\theta_k C(v_k)=A\sqrt{2(1+\varepsilon)}/(1+\delta)$, which is $\le\eta_\delta$ for $A$ small (bounded case: $\theta_k c\to0$). Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_refined_freedman} gives $\mathbb{P}(s_k)\le\exp(-\lambda_k^2/(2(1+\delta)v_k)) =\exp(-\tfrac{1+\varepsilon}{1+\delta}\log\log v_k)$, summable by Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_tail_summable}'s argument since $(1+\varepsilon)/(1+\delta)>1$. Borel--Cantelli finishes.

nodes.name: Sharp general martingale LIL
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a square-integrable martingale with $M_0=0$, $\langle M\rangle_n\to\infty$ a.s., satisfying \textbf{(H)} (in particular any bounded-increment martingale). Then \[ \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{M_n}{\sqrt{2\,\langle M\rangle_n\,\log\log\langle M\rangle_n}} \ \le\ 1\qquad\text{a.s.}, \] and, applied to $-M$ (same quadratic variation, Definition~\ref{def:pred_qv}), the two-sided bound $\limsup_n|M_n|/\sqrt{2\langle M\rangle_n\log\log\langle M\rangle_n}\le1$ a.s. (Formalized for bounded increments, both in the equivalent form ``a.s.\ for every $b>1$, eventually $|M_n|\le b\sqrt{2\langle M\rangle_n\log\log\langle M\rangle_n}$'' and as the genuine $\limsup$ statement \texttt{AlphaRAR.ae\_limsup\_abs\_div\_sqrt\_predQuadVar\_mul\_loglog\_le\_one}.)
nodes.label: thm:llil_sharp

nodes.statement: Fix a countable family $\eta_j\downarrow1$, $\varepsilon_j\downarrow0$ with $\varepsilon_j>\delta_j>0$. For each $j$, Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_sharp_block} and the repackaging of Theorem~\ref{thm:llil_bounded} give, a.s., $\limsup_n M_n/\sqrt{2\langle M\rangle_n\log\log\langle M\rangle_n}\le \sqrt{(1+\varepsilon_j)\eta_j}$. Intersect the countably many a.s.\ events and let $j\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Sharp LIL for growing increments with a linear quadratic variation
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a square-integrable martingale with $M_0=0$, increments bounded by a monotone nonnegative growth $|\Delta M_i|\le g(i)$ satisfying the base-independent condition \textbf{(H)} $g(n)\sqrt{L(n)/n}\to0$, and a \emph{linear} quadratic-variation bound $\langle M\rangle_n\le v\,n$ ($v>0$). Then, a.s., for every $\beta>1$ eventually $|M_n|\le\beta\sqrt{2v\,n\,L(n)}$, i.e.\ $\limsup_n|M_n|/\sqrt{2v\,n\,L(n)}\le1$.
nodes.label: thm:llil_growth_sharp

nodes.statement: Fix $\beta>1$ and block with the geometric horizons $N_j=\lceil\rho^j\rceil$ for $\rho=1+(\beta-1)/2\downarrow1$ and $\delta=(\beta-1)/2$, so $(1+\delta)\rho=\rho^2<\beta^2$.
