Over each block the increments are bounded by $g(N_j)$, and condition \textbf{(H)} transfers to the block form $g(N_j)\sqrt{\log(j+2)/N_j}\to0$ because $\log(j+2)\le(\log K+1)\,L(N_j)$ with $K=1/\log\rho+2$ (from $j\le\log N_j/\log\rho$), so the block quantity is $\le\sqrt{\log K+1}\,g(N_j)\sqrt{L(N_j)/N_j}\to0$. The refined per-block Freedman bound (Lemma~\ref{lem:llil_sharp_block}) with the near-optimal $\theta_j=\alpha\sqrt{\log(j+2)/N_j}$, $\alpha=C/((1+\delta)v)$, gives a summable $p$-series tail; repackaging via the least $j$ with $n\le N_j$ (so $N_j\le\rho n+1$ and additively $\log(j+2)\le D_\rho+L(n)$) yields the constant $\beta$. \emph{No random stopping time}: the linear bound $\langle M\rangle_n\le v\,n$ lets the deterministic horizon $N_j$ play the role of quadratic-variation stopping (contrast the general \textbf{(H)} Theorem~\ref{thm:llil_sharp}, whose constant-\textbf{(H)} increments would require it). Countable intersection over $\beta_m=1+1/(m+1)\downarrow1$ and the two-sided step (apply to $-M$) give the $\limsup$ form.

nodes.name: Two-sided normalized bound
nodes.statement: Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:llil_general} (or \ref{thm:llil_bounded}), almost surely $|M_n|\le C\sqrt{\langle M\rangle_n\log\log\langle M\rangle_n}$ for all large $n$, some deterministic $C$. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:llil_bounded} to $M$ and $-M$. (Formalized for bounded increments; the \textbf{(H)} version follows once Theorem~\ref{thm:llil_general} is formalized.)
nodes.label: cor:llil_norm

nodes.name: Bound at scale $\sqrt{n\log\log n}$
nodes.statement: If moreover $\langle M\rangle_n\le K n$ for a constant $K$ (e.g.\ $|\Delta M_i|\le c$ gives $\langle M\rangle_n\le c^2 n$, Lemma~\ref{lem:qv_linear_bound}), then almost surely $|M_n|\le C'\sqrt{n\log\log n}$ for all large $n$.
nodes.label: cor:llil_nat

nodes.statement: $\langle M\rangle_n\le Kn$ gives $\log\log\langle M\rangle_n\le\log\log(Kn)\le \log\log n+o(1)$ for large $n$; substitute into Corollary~\ref{cor:llil_norm}.

nodes.name: The bounded-increment version is unconditional
nodes.statement: The normalized Corollary~\ref{cor:llil_norm} (\texttt{AlphaRAR.ae\_eventually\_abs\_le\_sqrt\_pred QuadVar\_mul\_loglog}) --- and hence \texttt{ae\_eventually\_abs\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_loglog} --- carries the standing hypothesis $\langle M\rangle_n\to\infty$. For a \emph{bounded-increment} martingale this hypothesis is \emph{unnecessary and can genuinely fail}: a deterministic path (all selection probabilities in $\{0,1\}$) has $\langle M\rangle\equiv0$, yet $M\equiv0$ is trivially $O(\sqrt{n\log\log n})$. The version \texttt{AlphaRAR.ae\_eventually\_abs\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_loglog \_of\_bdd} drops $\langle M\rangle\to\infty$ entirely: it applies the deterministic-horizon growing-increment engine \texttt{ae\_eventually\_abs\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_loglog\_of\_growing}, whose only quadratic-variation input is the \emph{linear} bound $\langle M\rangle_n\le c^2n$ (\texttt{predQuadVar\_le\_of\_bound}), with parameters $\alpha=1/c$, $C=3c$, $v=c^2$ satisfying its admissibility (via $\log(j+2)\le 2^j$) and summability (exponent $1<2$). This is the form the possibly-degenerate assignment martingale requires.
nodes.label: rem:llil_bdd_uncond

nodes.name: Partial sums of independent centred variables form a martingale
nodes.statement: Let $(Y_j)_{j\ge0}$ be independent, integrable and centred ($\mathbb{E} Y_j=0$). Then the partial sums $S_n=\sum_{j<n}Y_j$ are a martingale with $S_0=0$, for the ``strictly before $n$'' natural filtration $\mathcal{F}_n=\sigma(Y_0,\dots,Y_{n-1})$ (with $\mathcal{F}_0$ trivial).
nodes.label: lem:hw_martingale

nodes.statement: $S_n$ is $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable (a sum of $Y_0,\dots,Y_{n-1}$) and integrable. For the increment, $\mathbb{E}[S_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_n]=S_n+\mathbb{E}[Y_n\mid\mathcal{F}_n]=S_n+\mathbb{E} Y_n=S_n$, because $Y_n$ is independent of the past $\mathcal{F}_n=\sigma(Y_0,\dots,Y_{n-1})$. Mathlib's $\log\log$-free \texttt{condExp\_indep\_eq} supplies $\mathbb{E}[Y_n\mid\mathcal{F}_n]=\mathbb{E} Y_n$; the ``strictly before'' index is what makes $S_0=0$ (unlike \texttt{Filtration.natural}, which would force $S_0=Y_0$).

nodes.name: Quadratic variation of the i.i.d.\ sum
nodes.statement: In the setting of Lemma~\ref{lem:hw_martingale}, if additionally $\mathbb{E}[Y_j^2]<\infty$, the predictable quadratic variation has increment $\langle S\rangle_{n+1}-\langle S\rangle_n=\mathbb{E}[Y_n^2]$; hence if $\mathbb{E}[Y_j^2]\le v$ for all $j$, then $\langle S\rangle_n\le v\,n$ almost surely for all $n$.
nodes.label: lem:hw_qv

nodes.statement: The increment of $\langle S\rangle$ is the conditional second moment of $\Delta S_n=Y_n$ (\texttt{predQuadVar\_succ\_sub\_eq}), which independence makes the constant $\mathbb{E}[Y_n^2]$ (\texttt{condExp\_natFiltLT\_comp\_indep} with $g=(\cdot)^2$); telescoping from $\langle S\rangle_0=0$ gives $\langle S\rangle_n=\sum_{j<n}\mathbb{E}[Y_j^2]\le v\,n$. Applied with $S=\tilde S$ and $v=\sigma^2$ (since $\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(Y_j^{\mathrm L})\le\sigma^2$) this is the linear bound $\langle\tilde S\rangle_n\le \sigma^2 n$ the growing-increment LIL requires.

nodes.name: Loglog LIL for bounded i.i.d.\ increments
nodes.statement: Let $(Y_j)$ be independent and centred with $|Y_j|\le c$ a.e.\ and second moments bounded below, $\mathbb{E}[Y_j^2]\ge w>0$. Then $S_n=\sum_{j<n}Y_j$ satisfies $|S_n|=O(\sqrt{n\log\log n})$ a.s.
nodes.label: cor:hw_bounded

nodes.statement: $S$ is a martingale (Lemma~\ref{lem:hw_martingale}) with bounded increments $|\Delta S_j|=|Y_j|\le c$; its quadratic variation is $\langle S\rangle_n=\sum_{j<n}\mathbb{E}[Y_j^2]$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:hw_qv}), so $\langle S\rangle_n\ge w\,n\to\infty$. The bounded-increment loglog LIL (Corollary~\ref{cor:llil_nat}) applies directly. This is the special case of Theorem~\ref{thm:hw} where no truncation is needed, and is already fully formalized.

nodes.name: Three-level truncated decomposition
nodes.statement: Low cutoff $b_j:=\sqrt{j/\log(j+2)}$ (the \emph{log}-level scale, strictly below the LIL scale $\sqrt{j/L(j)}$) and high cutoff $\sqrt j$. Split each increment into low, medium and high parts, \[ Y_j^{\mathrm L}:=Y_j\mathbf{1}_{\{|Y_j|\le b_j\}},\quad Y_j^{\mathrm M}:=Y_j\mathbf{1}_{\{b_j<|Y_j|\le\sqrt j\}},\quad Y_j^{\mathrm H}:=Y_j\mathbf{1}_{\{|Y_j|>\sqrt j\}}, \] so $Y_j=Y_j^{\mathrm L}+Y_j^{\mathrm M}+Y_j^{\mathrm H}$, and set \[ \tilde S_m:=\sum_{j\le m}\!\big(Y_j^{\mathrm L}-\mathbb{E} Y_j^{\mathrm L}\big),\quad W_m:=\sum_{j\le m}\!\big(Y_j^{\mathrm M}-\mathbb{E} Y_j^{\mathrm M}\big),\quad H_m:=\sum_{j\le m}Y_j^{\mathrm H},\quad D_m:=\sum_{j\le m}\mathbb{E}\big[Y_j\mathbf{1}_{\{|Y_j|\le\sqrt j\}}\big]. \] Since $\mathbb{E} Y_j^{\mathrm L}+\mathbb{E} Y_j^{\mathrm M}=\mathbb{E}[Y_j\mathbf{1}_{\{|Y_j|\le\sqrt j\}}]$, one has $S_m=\tilde S_m+W_m+H_m+D_m$.
nodes.label: def:hw_trunc

nodes.name: High part is eventually zero
nodes.statement: Almost surely $Y_j^{\mathrm H}=0$ for all large $j$, so $H_m$ is eventually constant and $H_m=O(1)$ a.s. (The formalized statement is the equivalent substance: almost surely $|Y_j|\le\sqrt j$ for all large $j$, whence $Y_j^{\mathrm H}=Y_j\mathbf{1}_{\{|Y_j|>\sqrt j\}}=0$.)
nodes.label: lem:hw_high

nodes.statement: $\sum_j\mathbb{P}(|Y_j|>\sqrt j)=\sum_j\mathbb{P}(Y_1^2>j)\le\mathbb{E}[Y_1^2]+1<\infty$ by the layer-cake bound (Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc_tail_summable}). The first Borel--Cantelli lemma places a.e.\ $\omega$ in only finitely many $\{|Y_j|>\sqrt j\}$; past that index $Y_j^{\mathrm H}=0$.

nodes.name: Sharp low-part LIL
nodes.statement: $\tilde S$ is a martingale with $|\Delta\tilde S_j|\le2b_j$ and $\langle\tilde S\rangle_m=\sum_{j<m}\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(Y_j^{\mathrm L})\le\sigma^2 m$. With the log-level cutoff $b_j=\sqrt{j/\log(j+2)}$ the increments satisfy condition \textbf{(H)} in the sharp $\to0$ form, $2b_n\sqrt{L(n)/n}=2\sqrt{L(n)/\log(n+2)}\to0$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:llil_growth_sharp} gives, a.s., for every $\beta>1$ eventually $|\tilde S_m|\le\beta\sqrt{2\sigma^2 m\,L(m)}$, i.e.\ $\limsup_m|\tilde S_m|/\sqrt{2\sigma^2 m\,L(m)}\le1$.
nodes.label: lem:hw_low_H

nodes.statement: $|\Delta\tilde S_j|=|Y_j^{\mathrm L}-\mathbb{E} Y_j^{\mathrm L}|\le2b_j$ (\texttt{abs\_truncation\_sub\_integral\_le}), with $j\mapsto b_j$ monotone and nonnegative; the base-independent condition \textbf{(H)} $2b_n\sqrt{L(n)/n}= 2\sqrt{L(n)/\log(n+2)}\to0$ holds because $L(n)/\log(n+2)\to0$. The martingale $\tilde S$ (\texttt{martingale\_centeredTruncation}) has the linear quadratic-variation bound $\langle\tilde S\rangle_m\le\sigma^2 m$ (\texttt{predQuadVar\_centeredTruncation\_le}, via \texttt{integral\_truncation\_sub\_integral\_sq\_le} for $\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(Y^{\mathrm L})\le\sigma^2$). These three feed the sharp growing-increment engine (\texttt{ae\_eventually\_abs\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_loglog\_of\_growth\_sharp\_all}) with growth $g=2b$; the block scheme uses deterministic horizons $N_j=\lceil\rho^j\rceil$ with $\rho\downarrow1$, so \emph{no random stopping time} is needed --- the linear bound $\langle\tilde S\rangle\le\sigma^2 m$ lets a deterministic time horizon play the role of quadratic-variation stopping. The upper bound uses only $\langle\tilde S\rangle_m\le\sigma^2 m$; that $\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(Y_j^{\mathrm L})\to\sigma^2$ (so $\langle\tilde S\rangle_m/(\sigma^2 m)\to1$) is not needed for $\limsup\le1$, but confirms the constant is sharp.

nodes.name: Medium variance series converges under a bare second moment
nodes.statement: $\displaystyle\sum_{j\ge3}\frac{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(Y_j^{\mathrm M})}{j\,L(j)}<\infty$.
nodes.label: lem:hw_medium_var

nodes.statement: $\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(Y_j^{\mathrm M})\le\mathbb{E}[(Y_j^{\mathrm M})^2]=\mathbb{E}[Y^2\mathbf{1}_{\{b_j<|Y|\le\sqrt j\}}]$, so by Tonelli \[ \sum_{j\ge3}\frac{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(Y_j^{\mathrm M})}{j\,L(j)}\ \le\ \mathbb{E}\Big[Y^2\!\!\sum_{j:\,b_j<|Y|\le\sqrt j}\frac{1}{j\,L(j)}\Big]. \] Fix $y=|Y|$. With the log-level cutoff $b_j=\sqrt{j/\log(j+2)}$ the condition $b_j<y\le\sqrt j$ means $y^2\le j$ and $j/\log(j+2)<y^2$; as $t\mapsto t/\log(t+2)$ is increasing the latter is $j<j_0(y)$, where $j_0(y)/\log(j_0(y)+2)=y^2$, so $j_0(y)\asymp y^2\log(y^2)$. Thus $j$ runs over $[y^2,j_0(y))$, an interval of multiplicative width $\asymp\log(y^2)$ on which $L(j)\asymp L(y^2)$; hence \[ \sum_{y^2\le j<j_0(y)}\frac{1}{j\,L(j)}\ \asymp\ \frac{1}{L(y^2)}\log\frac{j_0(y)}{y^2}\ \asymp\ \frac{\log\log(y^2)}{L(y^2)}\ =\ O(1), \] bounded uniformly in $y$. The inner factor being bounded, the double sum is $\le C\,\mathbb{E}[Y^2]<\infty$. The mechanism: the medium band is only a $\log$-factor wide, so the harmonic inner sum is $O(\log\log/\log\log)=O(1)$; this is exactly where the bare second moment suffices. (The LIL-scale low cutoff $\sqrt{j/L(j)}$ would make the band a mere $\log\log$-factor wide and the inner sum $\to0$; the log-level cutoff trades that slack for the sharp-constant condition \textbf{(H)}$\to0$ of the low part, and $O(1)$ still gives convergence.) \emph{Formalization.} Both the analytic heart and the measure-theoretic wrapper are formalized. The uniform inner-sum bound $\sum_{j:\,t\le j<t\log(j+2)}1/(j\,L(j))\le C$ (with $t=y^2$) is \texttt{AlphaRAR.medium\_inner\_tsum\_le}, built from \texttt{AlphaRAR.medium\_sum\_Icc\_big} (the $t\ge9$ estimate: pull out $1/L(\lceil t\rceil)$ and bound the harmonic sum by $\log(B/A)\le\log(5\log t)=\log5+L(t)$) via the range bounds \texttt{medium\_crude} ($j<8t^2$) and \texttt{medium\_tight} ($j<t(\log9+2\log t)$), the harmonic comparison \texttt{sum\_Icc\_one\_div\_le}, and \texttt{loglog\_le\_loglog}. The wrapper \texttt{AlphaRAR.medium\_variance\_series\_le} turns it into the second-moment series: by finite-sum linearity $\sum_{j<n}\big(\int X^2\mathbf{1}_{\{b_j<|X|\le\sqrt j\}}\big)/(j\,L(j))=\int X^2\sum_{j<n} \mathbf{1}_{\{\dots\}}/(j\,L(j))$, the inner sum is $\le C$ pointwise (at $t=X(\omega)^2$, using $b_j<|x|\le\sqrt j\iff x^2\le j<x^2\log(j+2)$), so each partial sum is $\le C\,\mathbb{E}[X^2]$ and $\sum'_j(\dots)\le C\,\mathbb{E}[X^2]$ with the series summable. The reduction $\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(X\mathbf{1}_{\{b_j<|X|\le\sqrt j\}})\le\mathbb{E}[(X\mathbf{1}_{\{\dots\}})^2]=\mathbb{E}[X^2\mathbf{1}_{\{\dots\}}]$ (\texttt{variance\_le\_expectation\_sq}, $(X\mathbf{1}_S)^2=X^2\mathbf{1}_S$) plus comparison of nonnegative series (\texttt{Summable.of\_nonneg\_of\_le}) gives \texttt{AlphaRAR.medium\_variance\_summable}: $\sum_{j\ge3}\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(X\mathbf{1}_{\{b_j<|X|\le\sqrt j\}})/(j\,L(j))<\infty$. Taking $X=Y_0$ and using $\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(Y_j^{\mathrm M})=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(Y_0\mathbf{1}_{\{b_j<|Y_0|\le\sqrt j\}})$ (identical distribution) is the stated series.

nodes.name: Medium part is negligible
nodes.statement: $W_m=o(\sqrt{m\,L(m)})$ a.s. (precisely, $W_m/\sqrt{2(m+3)L(m+3)}\to0$, and $\sqrt{2(m+3)L(m+3)}\sim\sqrt{2m\,L(m)}$).
nodes.label: lem:hw_medium

nodes.statement: Put $a_j:=\sqrt{2\,j\,L(j)}$, positive nondecreasing with $a_j\to\infty$. The partial sums of the independent, mean-zero terms $(Y_j^{\mathrm M}-\mathbb{E} Y_j^{\mathrm M})/a_{j+1}$ form an $L^2$-bounded martingale, since by independence and Lemma~\ref{lem:hw_medium_var} \[ \int\Big(\sum_{j<n}\tfrac{Y_j^{\mathrm M}-\mathbb{E} Y_j^{\mathrm M}}{a_{j+1}}\Big)^2 =\sum_{j<n}\frac{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(Y_j^{\mathrm M})}{a_{j+1}^2} \le\tfrac12\sum_{j}\frac{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(Y_j^{\mathrm M})}{j\,L(j)}<\infty . \] Hence $\sum_j(Y_j^{\mathrm M}-\mathbb{E} Y_j^{\mathrm M})/a_{j+1}$ converges a.s.\ by the $L^2$ martingale convergence theorem (Lemma~\ref{lem:slln_l2_conv}), and Kronecker's lemma with weights $b_j=a_j$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:kronecker_general}, whose conclusion $a_m^{-1}\sum_{j<m}a_{j+1}y_j\to0$ with $y_j=(Y_j^{\mathrm M}-\mathbb{E} Y_j^{\mathrm M})/a_{j+1}$ is exactly $a_m^{-1}\sum_{j<m}(Y_j^{\mathrm M}-\mathbb{E} Y_j^{\mathrm M})\to0$) gives $W_m=o(a_m)=o(\sqrt{m\,L(m)})$ a.s. This is the Kolmogorov-convergence-plus-Kronecker pattern of the martingale SLLN (Chapter~\ref{chap:pre_slln}); both ingredients are already formalized.

nodes.name: Drift is negligible
nodes.statement: $|D_m|\le2\sigma^2\sqrt m$, so $D_m=O(\sqrt m)=o(\sqrt{m\,L(m)})$. (The formalized statement is the deterministic core $|\sum_{j<m}\!\int\operatorname{trunc}(X,\sqrt j)|\le2(\int X^2)\sqrt m$ for a single centred $X$; since the i.i.d.\ $Y_j$ share the law of $X$, $D_m=\sum_{j<m}\!\int \operatorname{trunc}(X,\sqrt j)$ and this is exactly $|D_m|\le2\sigma^2\sqrt m$.)
nodes.label: lem:hw_drift

nodes.statement: Each summand $\mathbb{E}[Y_j\mathbf{1}_{\{|Y_j|\le\sqrt j\}}]$ is the mean of the truncation of the centred $Y_j$ at level $\sqrt j$, so the already-formalized centred truncated-mean bound $|\!\int\operatorname{trunc}(X,A)|\le\mathbb{E}[X^2]/A$ (\texttt{AlphaRAR.abs\_integral\_truncation\_le}, about Mathlib's \texttt{MeasureTheory.truncation}) gives $|\mathbb{E}[Y_j\mathbf{1}_{\{|Y_j|\le\sqrt j\}}]|\le \sigma^2/\sqrt j$. Summing with $\sum_{j\le m}1/\sqrt j\le2\sqrt m$ (\texttt{AlphaRAR.sum\_one\_div\_sqrt\_le}, also formalized) gives $|D_m|\le2\sigma^2 \sqrt m$; and $\sqrt m/\sqrt{m\,L(m)}\to0$, so $D_m=o(\sqrt{m\,L(m)})$. Both cited bounds are exactly those used for the drift in the existing (log-rate) truncation route (Lemmas~\ref{lem:trunc_mean_bound}--\ref{lem:trunc_drift}), applied here at level $\sqrt j$ instead of $\sqrt i$.

nodes.name: i.i.d.\ Hartman--Wintner, upper half
nodes.statement: For i.i.d.\ $(Y_j)$ with $\mathbb{E}[Y_1]=0$ and $0<\mathbb{E}[Y_1^2]=\sigma^2<\infty$, almost surely \[ \limsup_{m\to\infty}\frac{S_m}{\sqrt{2\sigma^2 m\,\log\log m}}\ \le\ 1, \] in particular $S_m=O(\sqrt{m\log\log m})$; the two-sided form follows from $-Y$.
nodes.label: thm:hw

nodes.statement: By Definition~\ref{def:hw_trunc}, $S_m=\tilde S_m+W_m+H_m+D_m$, and the three remainders are $o(\sqrt{m\,L(m)})$: $H_m=O(1)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:hw_high}), $W_m=o(\sqrt{m\,L(m)})$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:hw_medium}) and $D_m=o(\sqrt m)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:hw_drift}). Hence $\limsup_m S_m/\sqrt{2\sigma^2 m\,L(m)}=\limsup_m\tilde S_m/\sqrt{2\sigma^2 m\,L(m)}\le1$ by the sharp low-part bound (Lemma~\ref{lem:hw_low_H}). No $A_0\to0$ limit (as in de~Acosta's LIL-scale truncation) is needed: the log-level cutoff $b_j\to\infty$ already gives $\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(Y_j^{\mathrm L})\to\sigma^2$, so the constant is sharp. The two-sided statement applies this to $-Y$. \emph{Formalization} (\texttt{AlphaRAR.iid\_hartmanWintner\_limsup\_le\_one}). Because Mathlib's \texttt{truncation} is half-open $(-b_j,b_j]$, the pointwise identity $Y_j=Y_j^{\mathrm L}+ Y_j^{\mathrm M}+Y_j^{\mathrm H}$ fails only at the single boundary atom $\{Y_j=-b_j\}$, where the uncovered mass is $-b_j\le0$; \emph{dropping} it gives the one-sided pointwise bound $Y_j\le Y_j^{\mathrm L}+Y_j^{\mathrm M}+Y_j\mathbf{1}_{\{|Y_j|>\sqrt j\}}$ (\texttt{le\_lowMedHigh}), enough for the upper half. The drift picks up the atom in expectation, controlled by $\sum_j b_j\,\mathbb{P}(Y_j=-b_j)\le \mathbb{E}|Y_0|<\infty$ (\texttt{sum\_atom\_le}, using that the distinct $-b_j$ index disjoint events). A coboundedness-free core (\texttt{hw\_eventually}) proves ``a.s.\ $\forall\beta>1$ eventually $S_m\le\beta\sqrt{2\sigma^2 m\,L(m)}$''; applying it to $-Y$ gives the matching lower bound $S_m\ge-\beta\sqrt{2\sigma^2 m\,L(m)}$, which supplies the coboundedness needed to pass to the $\limsup$. The nondegeneracy $\sigma^2>0$ is used so the weight is eventually positive.

nodes.name: de~Acosta's one-shot alternative
nodes.statement: The bound $\limsup_m S_m/\sqrt{2\sigma^2 m\log\log m}\le1$ can instead be obtained in one stroke by de~Acosta's method \cite{deAcosta1983}, which avoids the three-level split and may be cleaner to formalize as a self-contained i.i.d.\ result. In that route Theorem~\ref{thm:hw} is proved directly, while the general Theorem~\ref{thm:llil_general} is still used for the genuinely martingale (bounded or \textbf{(H)}) applications --- notably the assignment martingale $M_{\cdot,k}$.
nodes.label: rem:hw_deacosta

nodes.name: Optional skipping
nodes.statement:
Consider an algorithm--environment sequence $(A_j,Y_j)_{j\ge0}$ in a stationary environment with per-arm reward kernel $
u$: the response $Y_j$ is drawn from $
u(A_j)$, independent of the history given the current arm (the action-augmented filtration $\mathcal{F}_{j-1}\vee\sigma(A_j)$). Fix an arm $k$ pulled infinitely often a.s., and let $	au_0<	au_1<\cdots$ enumerate the pulls $\{j:A_j=k\}$. Then the sampled responses $(Y_{	au_m})_{m\ge0}$ are i.i.d.\ with law $
u_k$.
nodes.section: 13.6 Optional skipping and the response martingale
nodes.label: lem:opt_skip

nodes.statement:
The classical optional-skipping argument, with the selector $D_j=\mathbf{1}_{\{A_j=k\}}$. Decompose over the value $j$ of the $m$-th pull time $	au_m$: the event $\{	au_m=j\}$ coincides a.s.\ with the predictable hit event $\{N_j=m,\ A_j=k\}$ (where $N_j=\#\{i<j:A_i=k\}$), which is measurable for the action-augmented $\sigma$-algebra at time $j$, and on it the conditional law of $Y_j$ is the constant $
u_k$ (	exttt{condExp\_feedback}). Hence, for any prefix and measurable sets $E_i$, $\mathbb{P}\! ig( igcap_{i<N}Y_{	au_i}^{-1}E_i ig)=\prod_{i<N}
u_k(E_i)$ by induction on $N$, peeling the newest sample and summing over its a.s.-covering, pairwise-disjoint pull events; this is independence together with each marginal $=
u_k$. \emph{Formalization.} The combinatorial core is generic (	exttt{AlphaRAR.iIndepFun\_sampledSeq}, 	exttt{map\_sampledSeq\_eq}): for a predictable $\{0,1\}$-selector $D$ and a process $Y$ whose value is $ho$-fresh given the current $\sigma$-algebra on $\{D_j=1\}$ (	exttt{hfact}: $\mu(Y_j^{-1}E\cap S)=ho(E)\,\mu(S)$ for $S\subseteq\{D_j=1\}$), the samples at the hit times of $D$ are i.i.d.\ $ho$. The hit time $	au_m$ is 	exttt{Nat.nth}, and the honestly $\sigma$-algebra-measurable hit events replace the (absent from Mathlib) random stopping-time $\sigma$-algebra. The freshness 	exttt{hfact} is discharged for the response process (	exttt{hfact\_stationaryEnv}) from the stationary-environment conditional distribution. This general statement is not yet in Mathlib and is a worthwhile contribution.

nodes.name: LIL for a predictably-sampled i.i.d.\ sum
nodes.statement: In the setting of Lemma~\ref{lem:opt_skip}, write $D_j=\mathbf{1}_{\{A_j=k\}}$, let $\theta_k$ be the mean of $\nu_k$ and $N_n=\sum_{j<n}D_j$ (the number of pulls of arm $k$ before $n$). If $\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(\nu_k)=V<\infty$, then almost surely \[ \Big|\sum_{j<n}D_j(Y_j-\theta_k)\Big|\ =\ O\!\big(\sqrt{N_n\,\log\log N_n}\big). \]
nodes.section: 13.6 Optional skipping and the response martingale
nodes.label: cor:subsampled_lil

nodes.statement:
Reindexing the nonzero summands, $\sum_{j<n}D_j(Y_j-	heta_k)=S_{N_n}$ with $S_m:=\sum_{i<m}(Y_{	au_i}-	heta_k)$. By Lemma~ef{lem:opt_skip} the $(Y_{	au_i})$ are i.i.d.\ with law $
u_k$, so $S$ is an i.i.d.\ centred sum with variance $V$; since $N_n	o\infty$ a.s., Theorem~ef{thm:hw} (two-sided) gives $|S_{N_n}|=O(\sqrt{N_n\log\log N_n})$. \emph{Formalization} (	exttt{AlphaRAR.abs\_respMart\_le\_sqrt\_nat\_mul\_loglog}). The formalized statement is the sharp two-sided form: a.s., for every $ eta>1$, eventually $|Q_{n,k}|\le eta\sqrt{2V\,N_{n,k}\log\log N_{n,k}}$. The reindexing $Q_{n,k}=S_{N_{n,k}}$ (	exttt{respMart\_eq\_sum\_sampledSeq}) is an exact pointwise identity proved by induction on $n$ (a pull advances the sample rank via 	exttt{Nat.nth\_count}). Hartman--Wintner is applied through the coboundedness-free \emph{eventually} core (	exttt{hw\_eventually}) to the centred samples and their negatives; the time-change $N_{n,k}	o\infty$ (	exttt{hitCount\_tendsto\_atTop}) transports the eventual bound. The i.i.d.\ hypotheses and law $
u_k$ of the samples come from Lemma~ef{lem:opt_skip}; the moments are transported to $
u_k$ by change of variables. Requires $\int x\,d
u_k$, $\int x^2\,d
u_k$ finite and $V=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}(
u_k)>0$.

nodes.name: Complex exponential expansion
nodes.statement: For all $x\in\mathbb{R}$, \[ \Big\| e^{ix} - \big(1 + ix - \tfrac{x^2}{2}\big)\Big\| \;\le\; \min\!\big(2x^2,\ |x|^3\big). \]
nodes.label: lem:clt_exp_bound

nodes.statement: Both bounds follow from a short integral tower for the map $x\mapsto e^{ix}$, using $\tfrac{d}{dx}e^{ix}=ie^{ix}$ and the fundamental theorem of calculus. First $\|e^{ix}-1\|=\|\int_0^x i e^{is}\,ds\|\le|x|$. Integrating, $\|e^{ix}-1-ix\|=\|\int_0^x i(e^{is}-1)\,ds\|\le\int_0^{|x|}s\,ds=x^2/2$. Integrating once more, $\|e^{ix}-1-ix+\tfrac{x^2}{2}\|=\|\int_0^x i(e^{is}-1-is)\,ds\| \le\int_0^{|x|}\tfrac{s^2}{2}\,ds=|x|^3/6$, which is the cubic bound. The quadratic bound is $\|e^{ix}-1-ix\|+\tfrac{x^2}{2}\le x^2/2+x^2/2=x^2$. The specific constant $1/6$ is not used downstream; any fixed constant on the cubic term suffices.

nodes.name: A real elementary bound, unbounded form
nodes.statement: For every $y\ge0$, $\ \big|e^{y}(1-y)-1\big|\le y^2 e^{y}$.
nodes.label: lem:clt_real_exp_bound_pos

nodes.statement: As above $\big|e^{y}(1-y)-1\big|=g(y)=1-e^{y}(1-y)\ge0$. Since $1-y+y^2\ge0$ and $e^{y}\ge1+y$, we get $e^{y}(1-y+y^2)\ge(1+y)(1-y+y^2)=1+y^3\ge1$, i.e. $e^{y}(1-y)+y^2e^{y}\ge1$, which rearranges to $g(y)\le y^2 e^{y}$. This form is valid for all $y\ge0$ (not only $y\le1$); the factor $e^{y}$ is what is needed when $y=\tfrac{t^2}{2}v_{n,i}$ is only known to be bounded, not $\le1$.

nodes.name: Conditional characteristic increment
nodes.statement: Fix $t\in\mathbb{R}$. For each $n,i$ write \[ r_{n,i} := \mathbb{E}\big[e^{it\Delta_{n,i}}\mid\mathcal{F}_i\big] - \Big(1 - \tfrac{t^2}{2}\,v_{n,i}\Big). \] Then $\mathbb{E}[e^{it\Delta_{n,i}}\mid\mathcal{F}_i] = 1 - \tfrac{t^2}{2}v_{n,i} + r_{n,i}$ with \[ \|r_{n,i}\| \;\le\; \mathbb{E}\!\Big[\min\!\big(2t^2\Delta_{n,i}^2,\ |t|^3|\Delta_{n,i}|^3\big) \,\Big|\,\mathcal{F}_i\Big]. \]
nodes.label: lem:clt_cond_char

nodes.statement: Apply the conditional expectation to the pointwise identity $e^{it\Delta} = 1 + it\Delta - \tfrac{t^2}{2}\Delta^2 + \big(e^{it\Delta}-1-it\Delta+\tfrac{t^2}{2}\Delta^2\big)$. The linear term vanishes since $\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{n,i}\mid\mathcal{F}_i]=0$ (conditional expectation commutes with the coercion $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}$), and the quadratic term is $-\tfrac{t^2}{2}v_{n,i}$ by definition of $v_{n,i}$. The remainder $r_{n,i}$ is the conditional expectation of the last bracket, whose modulus is bounded pointwise by $\min(2t^2\Delta^2,\,|t|^3|\Delta|^3)$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_exp_bound} applied to $x=t\Delta$; conditional Jensen (\texttt{norm\_condExp\_le}) gives the stated bound.

nodes.name: Variance truncation
nodes.statement: Fix a constant $B$ with $\sigma^2<B$ (e.g.\ $B:=\sigma^2+1$). Define the stopped array by truncating increment $i$ as soon as the \emph{next} partial variance would exceed $B$: \[ \bar\Delta_{n,i}:=\Delta_{n,i}\,\mathbf{1}_{\{V_{n,i+1}\le B\}}, \qquad V_{n,i+1}=\textstyle\sum_{l\le i}v_{n,l}. \] The indicator is $\mathcal{F}_i$-measurable, since $V_{n,i+1}$ depends only on $v_{n,0},\dots,v_{n,i}$, all $\mathcal{F}_i$-measurable. Then: \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] $\bar\Delta_{n,i}$ is again a martingale difference array for $(\mathcal{F}_i)$, with per-step variances $\bar v_{n,i}=v_{n,i}\mathbf{1}_{\{V_{n,i+1}\le B\}}$; \item[(ii)] its predictable variation is bounded \emph{by the constant $B$}: $\bar V_n=\sum_{i<k_n}\bar v_{n,i}\le B$ everywhere; \item[(iii)] $\bar V_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}\sigma^2$, and $\bar\Delta_{n,i}$ satisfies the conditional Lindeberg condition; \item[(iv)] $P\big(\bar S_n\ne S_n\big)\le P(V_n>B)\to0$, where $\bar S_n=\sum_{i<k_n}\bar\Delta_{n,i}$. \end{enumerate} Consequently $S_n$ and $\bar S_n$ have the same characteristic-function limit, and it suffices to prove the theorem under the extra assumption $V_n\le B$ a.s.
nodes.label: lem:clt_truncation

nodes.statement: Since $v_{n,l}$ is $\mathcal{F}_l$-measurable and $l\le i$ for $l$ appearing in $V_{n,i+1}$, the indicator $\mathbf{1}_{\{V_{n,i+1}\le B\}}$ is $\mathcal{F}_i$-measurable; multiplying $\Delta_{n,i}$ by it therefore preserves both the $\mathcal{F}_{i+1}$- measurability and the martingale-difference property ($\mathbb{E}[\bar\Delta_{n,i}\mid\mathcal{F}_i]=\mathbf{1}_{\{V_{n,i+1}\le B\}}\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{n,i}\mid\mathcal{F}_i]=0$), and $\bar v_{n,i}=\mathbb{E}[\bar\Delta_{n,i}^2\mid\mathcal{F}_i]=\mathbf{1}_{\{V_{n,i+1}\le B\}}v_{n,i}$, proving (i). For (ii): because $V$ is nondecreasing, the retained indices $\{i:V_{n,i+1}\le B\}$ form a prefix $\{0,\dots,m\}$, and $\bar V_n=\sum_{i\le m}v_{n,i}=V_{n,m+1}\le B$ by the choice of $m$ --- there is no overshoot. For (iii): on $\{V_n\le B\}$ every indicator equals $1$, so $\bar V_n=V_n$ and $\bar S_n=S_n$; since $P(V_n\le B)\to1$ (as $V_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}\sigma^2<B$), both $\bar V_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}\sigma^2$ and (iv) follow, and the Lindeberg sum only decreases under truncation ($\bar\Delta_{n,i}^2\le\Delta_{n,i}^2$, $\{|\bar\Delta|>\varepsilon\}\subseteq\{|\Delta|>\varepsilon\}$). The final claim uses $\|\mathrm{charFun}(\mathrm{law}\,S_n)(t)-\mathrm{charFun}(\mathrm{law}\,\bar S_n)(t)\|\le 2P(S_n\ne\bar S_n)$.

nodes.name: Uniform smallness of the conditional variances
nodes.statement: For every $\varepsilon>0$ and every $i<k_n$, a.s. \[ v_{n,i}\;\le\;\varepsilon^2 + L_n(\varepsilon). \] In particular $\max_{i<k_n} v_{n,i}\le\varepsilon^2 + L_n(\varepsilon)$, so $L_n(\varepsilon)\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}0$ gives $\max_{i<k_n}v_{n,i}\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}0$.
nodes.label: lem:clt_max_var

nodes.statement: Split $v_{n,i}=\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{n,i}^2\mathbf{1}_{\{|\Delta_{n,i}|\le\varepsilon\}}\mid\mathcal{F}_i] +\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{n,i}^2\mathbf{1}_{\{|\Delta_{n,i}|>\varepsilon\}}\mid\mathcal{F}_i]$. The first conditional expectation is $\le\varepsilon^2$ (its integrand is $\le\varepsilon^2$ pointwise); the second is the $i$-th summand of $L_n(\varepsilon)$, hence $\le L_n(\varepsilon)$ since every summand is nonnegative (conditional expectation of a nonnegative function). The stated per-cell bound follows.

nodes.name: Sum of squared variances
nodes.statement: For every $\varepsilon>0$, a.s. \[ \sum_{i<k_n} v_{n,i}^2 \;\le\; \big(\varepsilon^2 + L_n(\varepsilon)\big)\,V_n . \] In particular, on $\{V_n\le B'\}$ with $L_n(\varepsilon)\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}0$, this gives $\sum_{i<k_n}v_{n,i}^2\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}0$.
nodes.label: lem:clt_sum_var_sq

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_max_var}, $v_{n,i}\le\varepsilon^2+L_n(\varepsilon)$ a.s.; since also $v_{n,i}\ge0$, this gives $v_{n,i}^2\le v_{n,i}(\varepsilon^2+L_n(\varepsilon))$. Summing over $i$ and factoring, $\sum_i v_{n,i}^2\le(\varepsilon^2+L_n(\varepsilon))\sum_i v_{n,i} =(\varepsilon^2+L_n(\varepsilon))V_n$.

nodes.name: Sum of the remainder majorants
nodes.statement: For every $\varepsilon\ge0$, a.s. \[ \sum_{i<k_n}\mathbb{E}\!\big[\min(2t^2\Delta_{n,i}^2,\,|t|^3|\Delta_{n,i}|^3)\mid\mathcal{F}_i\big] \;\le\; |t|^3\varepsilon\,V_n + 2t^2 L_n(\varepsilon). \] By Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_cond_char} the left-hand side dominates $\sum_{i<k_n}\|r_{n,i}\|$; hence on $\{V_n\le B'\}$ with $L_n(\varepsilon)\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}0$, $\sum_{i<k_n}\|r_{n,i}\|\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}0$ (send $n\to\infty$, then $\varepsilon\to0$).
nodes.label: lem:clt_sum_rem

nodes.statement: Pointwise, $\min(2t^2\Delta^2,|t|^3|\Delta|^3)\le |t|^3\varepsilon\,\Delta^2 + 2t^2\,\Delta^2\mathbf{1}_{\{|\Delta|>\varepsilon\}}$: on $\{|\Delta|\le\varepsilon\}$ use the cubic term ($|t|^3|\Delta|^3\le|t|^3\varepsilon\Delta^2$), on $\{|\Delta|>\varepsilon\}$ the quadratic term. Taking conditional expectations and summing over $i$ gives $|t|^3\varepsilon\sum_i v_{n,i}+2t^2 L_n(\varepsilon)$.

nodes.name: Almost-martingale expectation
nodes.statement: $\mathbb{E}[Z_{n,k_n}]\to1$ as $n\to\infty$.
nodes.label: lem:clt_Z_expectation

nodes.statement: The one-step increment factorises as $Z_{n,j+1}-Z_{n,j}=Z_{n,j}\big(\exp(it\Delta_{n,j}+\tfrac{t^2}{2}v_{n,j})-1\big)$, where the factor $Z_{n,j}$ is $\mathcal{F}_j$-measurable. Taking conditional expectation and using Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_cond_char}, \[ \mathbb{E}[Z_{n,j+1}-Z_{n,j}\mid\mathcal{F}_j] = Z_{n,j}\Big(e^{(t^2/2)v_{n,j}}\big(1-\tfrac{t^2}{2}v_{n,j}+r_{n,j}\big)-1\Big). \] Writing $y=\tfrac{t^2}{2}v_{n,j}\ (\le\tfrac{t^2}{2}B')$, the bracket splits as $\big(e^{y}(1-y)-1\big)+e^{y}r_{n,j}$; by Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_real_exp_bound_pos}, $|e^{y}(1-y)-1|\le y^2 e^{y} =\tfrac{t^4}{4}v_{n,j}^2\,e^{y}$. Hence the modulus is $\le|Z_{n,j}|\,e^{(t^2/2)B'}\big(\tfrac{t^4}{4}v_{n,j}^2+\|r_{n,j}\|\big)$. (The unbounded form of the elementary bound is essential here: $y$ is only bounded, not $\le1$.) Summing over $j$, telescoping and using the tower property $\mathbb{E}[Z_{n,k_n}-Z_{n,0}]=\sum_j\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}[Z_{n,j+1}-Z_{n,j}\mid\mathcal{F}_j]\big]$, \[ \big|\mathbb{E}[Z_{n,k_n}]-1\big| \le e^{(t^2/2)B'}\,\mathbb{E}\!\Big[\tfrac{t^4}{4}\textstyle\sum_j v_{n,j}^2 + e^{(t^2/2)B'}\sum_j\|r_{n,j}\|\Big]. \] Both sums tend to $0$ in probability (Lemmas~\ref{lem:clt_sum_var_sq},~\ref{lem:clt_sum_rem}) and are uniformly bounded, so by bounded convergence the expectations tend to $0$.

nodes.name: Characteristic function limit
nodes.statement: Under the two hypotheses ($V_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}\sigma^2$ and the conditional Lindeberg condition), for every $t\in\mathbb{R}$, \[ \mathbb{E}\big[e^{itS_n}\big]\;=\;\mathrm{charFun}(\mathrm{law}\,S_n)(t) \longrightarrow \exp\!\Big(-\tfrac{\sigma^2 t^2}{2}\Big). \]
nodes.label: lem:clt_product

nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_truncation} we may assume $V_n\le B'$ a.s. Then $e^{itS_n}=Z_{n,k_n}e^{-(t^2/2)V_n}$, so \[ \mathbb{E}[e^{itS_n}] - \exp(-\tfrac{t^2}{2}\sigma^2) = \mathbb{E}\big[Z_{n,k_n}\big(e^{-(t^2/2)V_n}-e^{-(t^2/2)\sigma^2}\big)\big] + e^{-(t^2/2)\sigma^2}\big(\mathbb{E}[Z_{n,k_n}]-1\big). \] The second term $\to0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_Z_expectation}. In the first, $|Z_{n,k_n}|\le e^{(t^2/2)B'}$ is bounded and $e^{-(t^2/2)V_n}-e^{-(t^2/2)\sigma^2}\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}0$ (continuity of $\exp$ and $V_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}\sigma^2$), so bounded convergence gives $\to0$.

nodes.name: Characteristic functions determine the limit
nodes.statement: The map sending a probability measure to its characteristic function is injective, and if $\mathbb{E}[e^{itX_n}]\to\exp(-\sigma^2 t^2/2)$ for all $t$, then $X_n$ converges in distribution to $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$.
nodes.label: lem:levy

nodes.statement: The target $\exp(-\sigma^2 t^2/2)$ is the characteristic function of $\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$ (\texttt{charFun\_gaussianReal}). Pointwise convergence of characteristic functions to that of a fixed probability measure implies weak convergence of the laws by the L\'evy continuity theorem (\texttt{ProbabilityMeasure.tendsto\_of\_tendsto\_charFun}); injectivity is \texttt{Measure.ext\_of\_charFun}. Together these give convergence in distribution to $\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$.

nodes.name: Martingale CLT, Lindeberg form
nodes.statement: Let $(\Delta_{n,i})_{i<k_n}$ be a martingale difference array (as in the standing setup) with predictable quadratic variation $V_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}\sigma^2$ and satisfying the conditional Lindeberg condition $L_n(\varepsilon)\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}0$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. Then the row sums converge in distribution, \[ S_n=\sum_{i<k_n}\Delta_{n,i} \;\overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow}\; \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2). \] In Lean the conclusion has the shape of Mathlib's i.i.d.\ central limit theorem: for every random variable $Y$ (on any probability space) with law $\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$, $S_n$ converges to $Y$ in distribution (\texttt{TendstoInDistribution}); the convergence of the laws of $S_n$ themselves is the case $Y=\mathrm{id}$ on $(\mathbb{R},\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2))$.
nodes.label: thm:mart_clt

nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:clt_product} gives pointwise convergence of the characteristic functions to that of $\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$; Lemma~\ref{lem:levy} converts this into convergence in distribution.

nodes.name: Per-arm self-normalized CLT
nodes.statement: Fix an arm $k$ with a limiting proportion $N_{n,k}/n\to v_k>0$ a.s.\ and per-step conditional variance $V_k>0$ (a finite second moment $\mathbb{E}|\xi_{1,k}-\theta_k|^2 = V_k<\infty$). Then the self-normalized response martingale converges in distribution, \[ \frac{Q_{n,k}}{\sqrt{V_k\,N_{n,k}}} \overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow} \mathcal N(0,1). \]
nodes.label: lem:mart_clt_selfnorm_arm

nodes.statement: Normalize $Q_{n,k}$ by the \emph{deterministic} $\sqrt{V_k v_k n}$: the increments $\Delta_{m}=X_{m,k}(\xi_{m,k}-\theta_k)/\sqrt{V_k v_k n}$ form a martingale-difference array (for the action-augmented filtration) whose predictable variation is $N_{n,k}/(v_k n)\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}1$ (consistency) and which satisfies the conditional Lindeberg condition, because the sampled responses are i.i.d.\ with finite variance $V_k$ (each cell contributes $\mathbf{1}\{A_m=k\}\,V_k^{-1}v_k^{-1}n^{-1}\mathbb{E}[(\xi-\theta_k)^2\mathbf{1}\{|\xi-\theta_k|>\varepsilon\sqrt{V_k v_k n}\}]$ and the truncated moment vanishes by dominated convergence). Theorem~\ref{thm:mart_clt} then gives $Q_{n,k}/\sqrt{V_k v_k n}\overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal N(0,1)$. Finally $\sqrt{V_k v_k n}/\sqrt{V_k N_{n,k}}=\sqrt{v_k n/N_{n,k}}\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}1$, so Slutsky yields the stated random-normalizer limit.

nodes.name: Joint componentwise CLT, deterministic normalization
nodes.statement: Suppose $N_{n,k}/n\to v_k$ a.s.\ for every arm $k$, with $v_k\ge0$ and $V_k\ge0$. Then the vector of deterministically-normalized response martingales converges jointly in distribution to a diagonal Gaussian, \[ \Big(\tfrac{Q_{n,1}}{\sqrt n},\dots,\tfrac{Q_{n,K}}{\sqrt n}\Big) \overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow} \mathcal N\!\big(0, \mathrm{diag}(v_1V_1,\dots,v_KV_K)\big). \]
nodes.label: lem:mart_clt_joint

nodes.statement: By the Cramér--Wold device it suffices to prove that every scalar projection converges: for each $w\in\mathbb{R}^K$, $\langle w, Q_n/\sqrt n\rangle = \big(\sum_k w_k Q_{n,k}\big)/\sqrt n$. The increments $\sum_k w_k X_{i,k}(\xi_{i,k}-\theta_k)$ form a single martingale-difference array (the arm indicators are disjoint, so the conditional square is $\sum_k w_k^2\mathbf{1}\{A_i=k\}V_k$, giving predictable variation $\sum_k w_k^2 V_k N_{n,k}/n\to\sum_k w_k^2 v_kV_k$; the conditional Lindeberg condition holds arm-by-arm by dominated convergence). Theorem~\ref{thm:mart_clt} yields $\big(\sum_k w_k Q_{n,k}\big)/\sqrt n\overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal N(0,\sum_k w_k^2 v_kV_k)$, which is precisely the projection $\langle w,\cdot\rangle$ of the diagonal Gaussian (whose covariance is $\mathrm{diag}(v_kV_k)$ by orthogonality of the coordinates, Lemma~\ref{lem:qv_orthogonal}). Cramér--Wold then gives the joint limit.

nodes.name: Joint componentwise CLT, self-normalized
nodes.statement: Suppose $N_{n,k}/n\to v_k$ a.s.\ for every arm $k$, with $v_k>0$. Then, under Condition~\textbf{A}, the vector of response martingales normalized by their own random counts converges jointly in distribution to a diagonal Gaussian, \[ \Big(\tfrac{Q_{n,1}}{\sqrt{N_{n,1}}},\dots,\tfrac{Q_{n,K}}{\sqrt{N_{n,K}}}\Big) \overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow} \mathcal N\!\big(0, \mathrm{diag}(V_1,\dots,V_K)\big). \]
nodes.label: lem:mart_clt_joint_selfnorm

nodes.statement: Write $Q_{n,k}/\sqrt{N_{n,k}}=(Q_{n,k}/\sqrt n)\cdot\sqrt{n/N_{n,k}}$. The deterministic-normalizer joint limit (Lemma~\ref{lem:mart_clt_joint}) gives $(Q_{n,k}/\sqrt n)_k\overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal N(0,\mathrm{diag}(v_kV_k))$, and the coordinatewise scaling vector $(\sqrt{n/N_{n,k}})_k\to(v_k^{-1/2})_k$ in probability (from $N_{n,k}/n\to v_k$ and $v_k>0$). Multivariate Slutsky (a continuous coordinatewise product against a constant limit) then sends the product to the image of $\mathcal N(0,\mathrm{diag}(v_kV_k))$ under the diagonal scaling $\mathrm{diag}(v_k^{-1/2})$, which is $\mathcal N(0,\mathrm{diag}(V_k))$.

nodes.name: Self-normalized componentwise form
nodes.statement: Suppose $N_{n,k}/n\to v_k$ a.s.\ with $v_k>0$ for every arm $k$ (so in particular $N_{n,k}\to\infty$). Then, under Condition~\textbf{A}, with $D_n=\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt{N_{n,1}},\dots,\sqrt{N_{n,K}})$, \[ D_n(\hat{\Theta}_n-\Theta)\overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal{N}(0,\mathrm{diag}(V_1,\dots,V_K)). \]
nodes.label: cor:mart_clt_componentwise

nodes.statement: By the exact Bahadur identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:estimator_bahadur}), $\hat\theta_{n,k}-\theta_k=(Q_{n,k}+(\theta_{0,k}-\theta_k))/(N_{n,k}+1)$, so \[ \sqrt{N_{n,k}}(\hat\theta_{n,k}-\theta_k) = \frac{Q_{n,k}}{\sqrt{N_{n,k}}}\cdot\frac{N_{n,k}}{N_{n,k}+1} + (\theta_{0,k}-\theta_k)\frac{\sqrt{N_{n,k}}}{N_{n,k}+1}. \] The self-normalized martingale vector $(Q_{n,k}/\sqrt{N_{n,k}})_k$ converges jointly to $\mathcal N(0,\mathrm{diag}(V_k))$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:mart_clt_joint_selfnorm}), while the two coordinatewise scaling factors tend to $1$ and $0$ in probability (as $N_{n,k}\to\infty$). Multivariate Slutsky (a continuous coordinatewise affine map against the constant limit $(1,0)$) therefore leaves the Gaussian limit unchanged.

nodes.name: Anscombe random-time self-normalized CLT
nodes.statement: Let $(\xi_i)_{i\ge0}$ be i.i.d.\ with mean $\mu$ and finite variance $v=\mathrm{Var}(\xi_0)$, and let $S_m=\sum_{i<m}(\xi_i-\mu)$. Let $(\tau_n)$ be positive-integer random indices for which there is a deterministic sequence $c_n\to\infty$ with $\tau_n/c_n\to1$ almost surely. Then \[ \frac{S_{\tau_n}}{\sqrt{\tau_n}} = \frac1{\sqrt{\tau_n}}\Big(\sum_{i<\tau_n}\xi_i-\tau_n\mu\Big) \;\overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow}\; \mathcal N(0,v). \]
nodes.label: lem:anscombe_clt

nodes.statement: Decompose $S_{\tau_n}/\sqrt{\tau_n}=(S_{c_n}/\sqrt{c_n})\cdot\sqrt{c_n/\tau_n}+(S_{\tau_n}-S_{c_n})/\sqrt{\tau_n}$. The base term $S_{c_n}/\sqrt{c_n}\overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal N(0,v)$ is the i.i.d.\ central limit theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:mart_clt}, in the form of the Lindeberg--L\'evy theorem) precomposed with the deterministic subsequence $c_n$; the scaling $\sqrt{c_n/\tau_n}\to1$ in probability by regularity, so Slutsky preserves the limit; and the window remainder $(S_{\tau_n}-S_{c_n})/\sqrt{\tau_n}\to0$ in probability, since on the event $|\tau_n-c_n|\le\varepsilon c_n$ (of probability $\to1$) the increment is bounded by the maximal increment over a window of length $\varepsilon c_n$, which is $O(\sqrt{\varepsilon c_n})$ in $L^1$ by Doob's maximal inequality; letting $\varepsilon\to0$ gives the claim. \emph{Formalization.} \texttt{AlphaRAR.tendstoInDistribution\_anscombe\_iid}, assembled from the base CLT along a subsequence (\texttt{tendstoInDistribution\_clt\_comp}, wrapping Mathlib's \texttt{tendstoInDistribution\_inv\_sqrt\_mul\_sum\_sub}), the negligibility of the window remainder (\texttt{AlphaRAR.tendstoInMeasure\_window}, via the Doob maximal inequality \texttt{AlphaRAR.mart\_maximal} on the i.i.d.-sum martingale \texttt{AlphaRAR.martingale\_iidSum}), and two Slutsky steps (\texttt{TendstoInDistribution.mul\_of\_tendstoInMeasure\_const}, Mathlib's \texttt{TendstoInDistribution.add\_of\_tendstoInMeasure\_const}). The regularity $\tau_n/c_n\to1$ is essential: for a general adaptive $\tau_n\to\infty$ the statement is false (one can freeze the self-normalized martingale above its typical value by pausing the index near a level crossing, using the law of the iterated logarithm). This lemma is the standalone martingale-CLT ingredient that Lemma~\ref{lem:componentwise} calls for, and the missing piece for the sparse componentwise CLT (Corollary~\ref{cor:sparse_clt}): with the per-arm regularity $N_{n,k}/c_{n,k}\to1$ supplied, applying it coordinatewise to the sampled response martingale $Q_{\cdot,k}$ yields $Q_{n,k}/\sqrt{N_{n,k}}\overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal N(0,V_k)$ even when $v_k=0$.

nodes.name: Per-arm self-normalized CLT, sparse
nodes.statement: Fix an arm $k$ sampled infinitely often, and suppose its pull count obeys the regularity $N_{n,k}/c_n\to1$ a.s.\ for some deterministic $c_n\to\infty$. Then, under Condition~\textbf{A}, \[ \frac{Q_{n,k}}{\sqrt{N_{n,k}}} \overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow} \mathcal N(0, V_k),\qquad V_k=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\mathrm{id};\nu_k]. \] No positivity of a limiting proportion is required, so this holds for sparse arms $v_k=0$.
nodes.label: lem:mart_clt_selfnorm_arm_sparse

nodes.statement: The sampled responses of arm $k$ are i.i.d.\ with mean $\theta_k$ and variance $V_k$ (a globally i.i.d.\ representative is \texttt{AlphaRAR.sampledClean}), and reindexing the pulls gives $Q_{n,k}=\sum_{i<N_{n,k}}(\xi_i-\theta_k)=S_{N_{n,k}}$ (\texttt{respMart\_eq\_sum\_sampledSeq}). Apply the Anscombe random-time CLT (Lemma~\ref{lem:anscombe_clt}) with $\tau_n=N_{n,k}$. \emph{Formalization.} \texttt{AlphaRAR.respMart\_selfNorm\_anscombe\_tendsto}: the clean-sample setup mirrors the LIL development (\texttt{iIndepFun\_sampledResponse}, \texttt{map\_sampledResponse\_eq}, \texttt{sampledSeq\_ae\_eq\_sampledClean}), supplying the i.i.d.\ hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:anscombe_clt}, and the almost-everywhere identity $S_{N_{n,k}}=Q_{n,k}$ transfers the limit law to $(\sqrt{N_{n,k}})^{-1}Q_{n,k}$.

nodes.name: Per-arm estimator CLT, sparse
nodes.statement: Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:mart_clt_selfnorm_arm_sparse}, $\sqrt{N_{n,k}}\,(\hat\theta_{n,k}-\theta_k)\overset{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal N(0,V_k)$. This is the componentwise statement of Corollary~\ref{cor:sparse_clt}.
nodes.label: lem:clt_theta_arm_sparse

nodes.statement: By the exact Bahadur identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:estimator_bahadur}), $\sqrt{N_{n,k}}(\hat\theta_{n,k}-\theta_k)=(Q_{n,k}/\sqrt{N_{n,k}})\cdot\frac{N_{n,k}}{N_{n,k}+1} + (\theta_{0,k}-\theta_k)\frac{\sqrt{N_{n,k}}}{N_{n,k}+1}$; the scaling factors tend to $1$ and $0$ in probability (as $N_{n,k}\to\infty$), and Slutsky applied to Lemma~\ref{lem:mart_clt_selfnorm_arm_sparse} gives the claim. \emph{Formalization.} \texttt{AlphaRAR.estimator\_sqrtN\_anscombe\_tendsto}, from \texttt{respMart\_selfNorm\_anscombe\_tendsto} via \texttt{estimator\_sub\_eq} and the two Slutsky lemmas \texttt{TendstoInDistribution.mul\_of\_tendstoInMeasure\_const}, \texttt{TendstoInDistribution.add\_of\_tendstoInMeasure\_const}.

nodes.name: Chi-square distribution
nodes.statement: For an integer $r\ge1$, the \emph{chi-square distribution with $r$ degrees of freedom} $\chi^2_r$ is the Gamma distribution with shape $r/2$ and rate $1/2$.
nodes.label: def:chiSquared

nodes.name: Square of a standard Gaussian
nodes.statement: If $Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ then $Z^2\sim\chi^2_1$.
nodes.label: lem:sq_gaussian_chisq1

nodes.statement: Compute the law of $Z^2$ by the change of variables $x = z^2$ on the standard Gaussian density; the resulting density $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi x}}e^{-x/2}$ on $(0,\infty)$ is the $\mathrm{Gamma}(1/2,1/2)$ density, i.e.\ $\chi^2_1$.

nodes.name: Additivity of Gamma laws
nodes.statement: If $U\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(a,\lambda)$ and $V\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(b,\lambda)$ are independent, then $U+V\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(a+b,\lambda)$.
nodes.label: lem:gamma_add

nodes.statement: The characteristic function of $\mathrm{Gamma}(a,\lambda)$ is $(1 - it/\lambda)^{-a}$; by independence the characteristic function of $U+V$ is the product $(1-it/\lambda)^{-(a+b)}$, which identifies the law by injectivity of characteristic functions.

nodes.name: Chi-square as a sum of squares
nodes.statement: If $Z_1,\dots,Z_r\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ are independent, then $\sum_{i=1}^r Z_i^2\sim\chi^2_r$.
nodes.label: lem:sum_sq_chisq

nodes.statement: Each $Z_i^2\sim\chi^2_1=\mathrm{Gamma}(1/2,1/2)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:sq_gaussian_chisq1}, and by independence and Lemma~\ref{lem:gamma_add} the sum is $\mathrm{Gamma}(r/2,1/2)=\chi^2_r$.

nodes.name: Rotation invariance of the standard Gaussian
nodes.statement: If $Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_K)$ and $O$ is an orthogonal $K\times K$ matrix, then $OZ\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_K)$.
nodes.label: lem:gaussian_rotation

nodes.statement: $OZ$ is Gaussian with mean $0$ and covariance $O I_K O^\top = I_K$. In Mathlib this is an instance of the invariance of \texttt{stdGaussian}/\texttt{IsGaussian} under orthogonal (more generally, measure-preserving linear) maps.

nodes.name: Diagonalization of an orthogonal projection
nodes.statement: An orthogonal projection matrix $P$ of rank $r$ can be written $P = O^\top \mathrm{diag}(I_r, 0)\, O$ for some orthogonal matrix $O$.
nodes.label: lem:proj_diag

nodes.statement: $P$ is symmetric and idempotent, hence diagonalizable in an orthonormal eigenbasis with eigenvalues in $\{0,1\}$, exactly $r$ of which are $1$. This is the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices, available in Mathlib.

nodes.name: Gaussian quadratic form under a projection
nodes.statement: Let $Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_K)$ and let $P$ be an orthogonal projection of rank $r$. Then $Z^\top P Z\sim\chi^2_r$.
nodes.label: thm:cochran

nodes.statement: Write $P = O^\top\mathrm{diag}(I_r,0)O$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:proj_diag}) and set $W = OZ$, which is $\mathcal{N}(0,I_K)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:gaussian_rotation}. Then $Z^\top P Z = W^\top\mathrm{diag}(I_r,0)W = \sum_{i=1}^r W_i^2$, which is $\chi^2_r$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:sum_sq_chisq}.
